lessons.title: What a Database Management System Is
lessons.content:
Imagine your school keeps every student's record in a big steel almirah full of khatas. One khata has names and roll numbers, another has exam marks, another has who paid the tuition fee. Now the headmaster asks a simple question: which students from Class 8 scored above 80 in maths and have not paid this month's fee? Someone has to open three khatas, flip hundreds of pages and match names by hand. It takes a whole afternoon, and a few mistakes sneak in. A database management system is the tool that answers that same question in a fraction of a second, with no mistakes. This course is about how such a system is built and how to use it well.

Data and information: Data means raw facts: 'Rina', '3.80', 'CSE', '01712-345678'. On their own they say very little. Information is data that has been organised so it means something: 'Rina, a CSE student, has a CGPA of 3.80'. A database turns piles of data into information that people can ask questions about. Keep this difference in mind, because the whole course is about storing data neatly so that getting information out is fast and correct.

What a database is: A database is a collection of related data, stored together on purpose, about some part of the real world. A university database stores students, teachers, courses and results. A bKash database stores accounts, balances and transactions. A Daraz database stores products, sellers, orders and deliveries. The key words are related and organised. A random folder of files on your laptop is data, but it is not really a database, because nothing ties the pieces together and nothing keeps them correct.

What a DBMS is: A database management system, or DBMS, is the software that creates the database, stores it, lets many people use it at the same time, keeps it correct, keeps it safe, and answers questions about it. Famous examples are MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle Database, Microsoft SQL Server and SQLite. SQLite is the small one hiding inside almost every Android phone and in browsers. The database plus the DBMS software together is often called a database system.

Before databases, the file-system way: In the 1960s, and still in many small offices today, each program kept its own files. The admission office had a file of students. The accounts office had another file with names and fees. The exam office had a third file with names and marks. Each program was written to read its own file format. This looks fine at first, but as the organisation grows, six big problems appear. Learning these problems is a classic exam question, because a DBMS exists to solve exactly these.

Problem 1, redundancy and inconsistency: The same fact is stored in many places. Rina's phone number is in the admission file, the accounts file and the exam file. That wastes space, but the worse part comes when Rina changes her number. The admission office updates it, the others forget. Now the university has two different phone numbers for the same girl, and nobody knows which is right. Having the same data in several copies is called redundancy, and copies that disagree are called inconsistency.

Problem 2, difficulty in getting answers: Suppose the vice chancellor wants a list of all students from Sylhet with CGPA above 3.5. No existing program does that. Someone must write a brand new program, or do it by hand. Every new question needs new code. In a DBMS, you just write one short query, like asking a question in a special language, and the answer comes back.

Problem 3, isolation of data: Data is scattered in different files with different formats: one uses commas, one uses fixed-width columns, one is an Excel sheet. Writing a program that combines them is painful. A DBMS keeps everything in one consistent structure, so combining is easy.

Problem 4, integrity problems: Rules like 'CGPA must be between 0 and 4' or 'every student must belong to an existing department' are buried inside program code. If a new program forgets the rule, bad data gets in. A DBMS lets you write the rule once in the database itself, and then every program, old or new, is forced to obey it.

Problem 5, atomicity problems: Say you send 500 taka from your bKash account to a friend. Two things must happen: take 500 from you and add 500 to your friend. If the power goes off after the first step, your money vanishes into thin air. With plain files there is no easy way to say 'do both or do neither'. A DBMS gives exactly that guarantee. All-or-nothing behaviour is called atomicity, and lessons 20 to 23 explain how it is done.

Problem 6, concurrent access and security: Two cashiers at a bank update the same account at the same moment. Each reads 1,000 taka, one adds 200, the other takes away 300, and each writes back its own answer. One update is lost. Files have no protection against this. Also, with files, anyone who can open the file sees everything, including salaries. A DBMS controls who sees what and makes many simultaneous users safe.

A database describes itself: One more difference from files is easy to miss. A data file is just bytes; only the program that wrote it knows that the first 20 characters are a name and the next 10 are a phone number. A DBMS stores, next to the data, a description of the data: which tables exist, which columns they have, their types and their rules. This description is called metadata, and the place it lives is called the catalog or data dictionary. Because the database carries its own description, any new program or tool can open it and understand it without secret knowledge.

What a DBMS gives you, in one list: less redundancy, consistent data, a query language to ask any question, integrity rules kept in one place, all-or-nothing transactions, safe sharing among many users, security and permissions, and backup and recovery after a crash. It also gives data independence, which means you can change how data is stored on disk without rewriting every program. Lesson 2 explains that idea with the three-schema architecture.

The price you pay: A DBMS is not free of cost. It needs more powerful hardware, trained people, and its general-purpose machinery adds some overhead. For a tiny shopping list on your phone, a plain text file is enough. For a hospital, a bank, a university or an e-commerce site, a DBMS is not optional. A good engineer knows when to use one and when not to, and that judgement is part of this course.

Who uses a database: Naive or end users click buttons in an app, like a student checking results on a university website, without knowing a database exists. Application programmers write the apps that talk to the database. Analysts and sophisticated users write their own queries to make reports. The database administrator, or DBA, is the boss of the database: decides the structure, gives permissions, sets up backups, watches performance and fixes problems. Database designers decide what tables to build before any data goes in.

A tiny worked example: Imagine a coaching centre in Mirpur. With files, it keeps students.txt with 'Rina, 01712345678, Physics' and fees.txt with 'Rina, 01712345678, paid'. Rina switches to a new SIM. Only students.txt is fixed, and now the SMS reminder about fees goes to her old number. With a DBMS, the phone number lives in one table, student, and the fee table only stores Rina's student ID. Change the number once, and every report everywhere shows the new number instantly.

A short history: In the 1960s came the hierarchical model, where data was stored as a tree, used in IBM's IMS, which helped the Apollo programme. Then came the network model, where records were linked by pointers like a web. Both were fast but painful, because to ask a question you had to know the exact path of pointers. In 1970, Edgar F. Codd at IBM proposed the relational model: store everything as simple tables and let the system figure out how to find things. Out of IBM's research came SQL in the 1970s, and Oracle sold one of the first commercial SQL databases in 1979. Relational databases have ruled ever since. From the 2000s, giant websites also started using NoSQL databases for huge scale, which you will meet in lesson 24.

Real-life example 1, a bKash payment: You pay 120 taka for a Pathao ride with bKash. The app sends a request to bKash's servers. The DBMS checks your PIN against stored data, checks your balance, takes 120 from your account and adds it to Pathao's account as one atomic transaction, writes a record in the transaction history, and does all this while lakhs of other people are paying at the same time. If the server crashes halfway, the DBMS's recovery system makes sure the money is either fully moved or not moved at all. You never think about any of this, which is the sign of a well-built database.

Real-life example 2, the result website: When HSC results come out, a huge number of students search by roll number at the same moment. Behind the website, a database stores every student's marks. Each search is a query: find the row where roll equals your roll, and show the grades. The DBMS uses an index, which is like the index at the back of a book, so it does not have to look through every row. That is why the answer can come back fast even though the table has well over a million rows. You will learn exactly how indexes work in lesson 17.

The course map: First you will learn to design a database: the ER model in lessons 3 and 4, and the relational model of tables in lesson 5. Then you will learn to ask questions: relational algebra in lesson 6 and SQL in lessons 7 to 12. Then you will learn good design theory: functional dependencies and normalization in lessons 13 to 15. Then you will look inside the engine: storage, indexes, query processing and optimization in lessons 16 to 19. Then you will learn how a DBMS stays correct with many users and crashes: transactions, concurrency and recovery in lessons 20 to 23. Finally come NoSQL, security and data warehouses.

Common mistakes and exam favourites: Students often mix up database and DBMS. The database is the data; the DBMS is the software that manages it. Another mix-up: thinking Excel is a DBMS. A spreadsheet stores tables, but it does not enforce rules between tables, does not handle many users safely, and has no proper transactions or recovery. Typical exam questions are: list the disadvantages of a file-processing system, give the advantages of a DBMS, describe the roles of a DBA, and define data, information, database and DBMS.

Recap: Data is raw facts, information is organised meaning. A database is related data stored on purpose, and a DBMS is the software that manages it. File systems suffer from redundancy, inconsistency, hard queries, scattered formats, integrity problems, no atomicity, unsafe concurrent use and weak security. A DBMS fixes all of these, at the cost of more complex software. Next lesson, you will see how a DBMS is organised inside, layer by layer.
key_points: Data is raw facts; information is data organised so it has meaning.
A database is a collection of related data; a DBMS is the software that creates, stores, protects and queries it.
File-processing systems suffer from redundancy, inconsistency, hard ad hoc queries, scattered formats, integrity problems, no atomicity, unsafe concurrent access and weak security.
A DBMS keeps rules in one place, gives a query language, all-or-nothing transactions, safe sharing, security and crash recovery.
The DBA designs the structure, grants permissions, plans backups and tunes performance.
Codd proposed the relational model in 1970; SQL grew out of it and relational databases still dominate.
A DBMS has a cost in hardware, skills and overhead, so tiny single-user data may not need one.
lessons.tip: Keep one example in your head for the whole course: a university with students, courses, departments and results. Every new idea in later lessons can be tried on this one example, and it will make the course feel like one story instead of 25 separate topics.
lessons.task: Take a sheet of paper and list five places in your daily life where a database must be working behind the scenes (for example bKash, the school result website, Daraz, a hospital, a phone contact list). For each, write two things it stores and one question someone might ask it, like 'which orders were not delivered yesterday?'.

quiz.q: Which of these is information rather than raw data?
options: Rina, a CSE student, has a CGPA of 3.80
quiz.explain: Single values like 3.80 or 'CSE' are raw data; information is data organised so it has a meaning, as in the full sentence about Rina.

quiz.q: Rina's phone number is updated in the admission file but not in the accounts file. Which file-system problem is this?
quiz.explain: The same fact is stored twice (redundancy), and the two copies now disagree (inconsistency).

quiz.q: Money is taken from your account but a power cut stops it from reaching your friend. Which DBMS property prevents this?
quiz.explain: Atomicity means a transaction happens completely or not at all, so a half-done transfer is undone.

quiz.q: Who proposed the relational model of data in 1970?
quiz.explain: Edgar F. Codd, working at IBM, published the relational model in 1970.

quiz.q: Which person is mainly responsible for permissions, backups and performance of a database?
quiz.explain: The DBA controls the database structure, grants and revokes access, plans backups and recovery, and tunes performance.

lessons.title: DBMS Architecture: Schemas, Data Independence and the Parts Inside
lessons.content:
Think of a big restaurant in Dhanmondi. As a customer you see only the menu and the plate on your table. The manager sees the full list of dishes, prices and suppliers. The kitchen staff see the fridge, the shelves and where each ingredient is kept. Same restaurant, three different views. If the kitchen moves the rice sacks to a new shelf, your menu does not change at all. A DBMS is built exactly like this, in layers, so that each kind of person sees only what they need and changes in one layer do not break the others. This lesson is about those layers and the machinery behind them.

Schema and instance: The schema is the design of the database: which tables exist, what columns they have, what types and rules. It is like the blank form for admission, with boxes for name, roll and department. The instance, also called the state or snapshot, is the actual data stored at one moment: the filled-in forms. The schema changes rarely, maybe once a semester when someone adds a column. The instance changes all the time, every time a student enrols or a grade is entered. In a sentence: schema is the shape, instance is the content.

A tiny example: The schema could be student(id, name, dept_id, cgpa, city). At 10 am the instance might have five rows: Rina, Sami, Tuli, Upol and Nadia. At 11 am a new student is admitted and the instance has six rows. The schema did not change; only the instance did. If the university decides to store each student's blood group too, the schema changes, because a new column, blood_group, is added to the design.

Why layers are needed: Different people need different views. A student should see only his own results. The accounts office needs fees but not exam marks. The DBA needs to know how data sits on the disk. Also, technology changes: today the data is on a hard disk, next year on SSDs, and the year after maybe spread across many servers. If every app had to know these storage details, every change would break every app. The answer is the three-schema architecture, proposed by the ANSI/SPARC committee in the 1970s.

The internal level: The bottom layer describes how data is physically stored: which files, how records are laid out in pages, which indexes exist, whether data is compressed. This description is called the internal schema or physical schema. Only the DBMS and the DBA care about it. For example, the internal schema might say: the student table is stored in a heap file, with a B+ tree index on id.

The conceptual level: The middle layer describes the whole database for the whole organisation: all the tables, all the columns, all the relationships and constraints, but no storage details. This is the conceptual schema, also called the logical schema. It says 'there is a student table with id, name, dept_id, cgpa and city, and dept_id must match a department'. It does not say where on disk anything lives. Database designers and the DBA work at this level.

The external level: The top layer has many external schemas, also called views or subschemas, one for each group of users. The exam office view might show student id, name and grades. The accounts view might show id, name and fee status. A student's portal shows only that student's own rows. Each user sees a small, tailored window into the database and nothing more. That also helps security: you cannot misuse data you cannot see.

A view in real SQL: Here is how the exam office view might be written: CREATE VIEW exam_view AS SELECT s.id, s.name, e.course_code, e.grade FROM student s JOIN enroll e ON s.id = e.student_id. After this, the exam office program simply runs SELECT * FROM exam_view WHERE id = 1 and sees Rina's grades, as if exam_view were a real table. It never sees city, CGPA or any fee data. The view is stored only as this definition, a saved question. Every time someone reads it, the DBMS runs the saved question on the real tables, so the view always shows fresh data. You will write many views in lesson 11.

Mappings between levels: The DBMS keeps two mappings. The external-conceptual mapping says how each view is built from the full logical tables. The conceptual-internal mapping says how each logical table is stored physically. When you ask a question through a view, the DBMS translates it down through these mappings to the real files. You never see this translation; it just works.

Logical data independence: This is the ability to change the conceptual schema without changing the external views or the application programs. Suppose the university adds a blood_group column to student, or splits a big table into two. As long as the DBMS can still build the old views from the new tables, the exam office app keeps working untouched. Only the external-conceptual mapping is updated.

Physical data independence: This is the ability to change the internal schema without changing the conceptual schema. The DBA can move the student table to a faster disk, add a new index on city, or change the file organisation. The tables, columns and queries stay exactly the same; queries may simply run faster. Physical independence is easier to achieve than logical independence, and modern relational systems give it almost completely. An easy way to remember: physical is about how it is stored, logical is about what is stored.

Data models: A data model is the set of ideas and tools used to describe data, relationships and rules. The relational model, used in this course, describes everything as tables. The entity-relationship model, used in lessons 3 and 4, is a picture-based model for designing. Older models are hierarchical (trees) and network (records linked by pointers). Object-based models add classes and inheritance. Semi-structured models, like JSON and XML documents, allow each record to have a slightly different shape. Different models suit different jobs.

Database languages: A DBMS offers a data definition language, DDL, to define schemas: create a table, add a column, drop a table. It offers a data manipulation language, DML, to work with the instance: insert, update, delete and query rows. In SQL, CREATE TABLE is DDL and SELECT or INSERT is DML. There is also data control language, DCL, for permissions, like GRANT and REVOKE. DML can be procedural, where you say step by step how to get the data, or declarative, where you only say what you want. SQL is mainly declarative: you say 'give me students with CGPA above 3.5', not how to scan the file.

Inside the DBMS, the query processor: When you send a query, it first goes to the parser, which checks the spelling and grammar and checks that the tables and columns exist, using the catalog. Then the query is translated into an internal form, usually a tree of relational algebra operations. The optimizer then looks at many possible ways to run it and picks a cheap one. Finally the execution engine runs that plan and produces the answer. Lessons 18 and 19 go deep into this.

Inside the DBMS, the storage manager: Below the query processor sits the storage manager. It has a file manager that handles space on disk, a buffer manager that brings disk pages into memory and decides which pages to keep, an authorization and integrity manager that checks permissions and rules, and a transaction manager that keeps the database correct during failures and when many users work at once. The transaction manager includes the concurrency control manager and the recovery manager, which you will meet in lessons 20 to 23.

The catalog, again: All schemas, views, constraints, user accounts and statistics live in the catalog, also called the data dictionary. The DBMS reads it constantly: the parser uses it to check names, the optimizer uses its statistics to guess costs, and the authorization manager uses it to check permissions. The catalog itself is usually stored as tables, so you can even query it.

Client-server architectures: In a one-tier setup, the app and the database live on the same machine, like a phone app using SQLite. In a two-tier setup, the client program talks directly to a database server over the network, like an old office accounts program connecting to a central MySQL server. In a three-tier setup, the client, usually a browser or mobile app, talks to an application server, which holds the business rules and is the only thing that talks to the database. Almost every website and big app today uses three tiers, because it is safer and easier to grow: the database is never exposed directly to the internet.

Real-life example 1, a university portal: Rina logs into her university portal from her phone. The phone app is the client. It sends her request to the application server, which checks her password and then asks the database for her results through a view that only shows her rows. The DBMS's query processor parses the request, the optimizer uses the index on student id, and the storage manager fetches the right pages into memory. Meanwhile the DBA has just moved the result table to a new SSD over the weekend. Rina notices nothing except that the page loads faster. That is physical data independence working for her.

Real-life example 2, a Daraz upgrade: Suppose Daraz decides to add a new column, delivery_slot, to the orders table so customers can choose a time. The old seller app, which shows only order id, product and quantity, keeps working without any change, because its view does not include the new column. Only new screens that want the delivery slot are updated. That is logical data independence: the logical design grew, and the old external views stayed the same.

Common mistakes and exam favourites: Students often mix up schema and instance; remember schema is the design, instance is the data right now. They also mix up the two independences: physical means storage changes do not affect the logical schema; logical means logical schema changes do not affect views and apps. Another trap: thinking views store their own copy of the data. A normal view stores only its definition; the data comes from the base tables. Typical exam questions: draw and explain the three-schema architecture, define both kinds of data independence with examples, list the components of a DBMS, and compare two-tier and three-tier architectures.

Recap: The schema is the design and the instance is the current data. The three-schema architecture has internal, conceptual and external levels, connected by mappings. Physical data independence protects the logical schema from storage changes, and logical data independence protects views and apps from logical changes. A DBMS uses DDL, DML and DCL, and is built from a query processor, a storage manager and a catalog. Most real systems use a three-tier architecture. Next, you will start designing databases with the entity-relationship model.
key_points: Schema is the design of the database; instance is the data stored at a particular moment.
The three-schema architecture has an internal (physical), a conceptual (logical) and an external (view) level.
Physical data independence: storage changes do not force changes to the logical schema.
Logical data independence: changes to the logical schema do not force changes to views or programs.
DDL defines schemas, DML reads and changes data, DCL controls permissions; SQL is mostly declarative.
A DBMS has a query processor (parser, optimizer, execution engine), a storage manager (file, buffer, authorization, transaction managers) and a catalog.
Three-tier architecture puts an application server between the client and the database.
lessons.tip: When you meet a new term in this course, ask yourself which level it belongs to: internal, conceptual or external. Indexes and files are internal, tables and constraints are conceptual, views are external. This habit sorts the whole subject in your head.
lessons.task: Pick an app you use, such as a food delivery app. On paper, draw three boxes: what the customer sees (external), what the company must store about all customers, restaurants and orders (conceptual), and one guess about how it might be stored (internal, for example 'orders sorted by date on SSD'). Then write one change that would be physical and one that would be logical.

quiz.q: A university adds a blood_group column to the student table. What has changed?
options: Nothing, columns are part of the instance
quiz.explain: Adding a column changes the design of the table, which is the schema. Entering data for students changes the instance.

quiz.q: The DBA moves a table to a faster disk and adds an index, and no query or program needs changing. This shows:
quiz.explain: Changing storage details without touching the logical schema is physical data independence.

quiz.q: Which level of the three-schema architecture shows a tailored part of the database to one group of users?
quiz.explain: The external level holds views or subschemas, each made for a particular user group.

quiz.q: Which component of a DBMS chooses a cheap way to run a query?
quiz.explain: The parser checks the query, but the optimizer compares possible plans and picks a low-cost one.

quiz.q: In a three-tier architecture, who talks directly to the database?
options: Nobody, the database talks to itself
quiz.explain: The client talks to the application server, and only the application server sends queries to the database.

lessons.title: The Entity-Relationship Model I: Entities, Attributes and Relationships
lessons.content:
Before a builder pours a single bag of cement, an architect draws the building on paper. Rooms, doors, which room connects to which. Fixing a mistake on paper costs a pencil eraser; fixing it after the walls are up costs lakhs of taka. Databases work the same way. Before creating tables, a designer draws a picture of the data: what things exist and how they are connected. The most famous way to draw that picture is the entity-relationship model, or ER model, proposed by Peter Chen in 1976. This lesson teaches its basic building blocks.

Why design first: Ask a shopkeeper in Gulistan what his business is about and he will talk in nouns and verbs: customers buy products, suppliers deliver stock, staff handle sales. The ER model captures exactly that. Nouns become entities, verbs become relationships, and the details about each noun become attributes. Talking in these terms lets a designer and a non-technical owner agree on the design before any code is written. The ER diagram is the shared language between them.

Entity: An entity is a thing in the real world that can be told apart from other things, and that we want to store data about. Rina is an entity. The course CSE101 is an entity. The Computer Science department is an entity. An entity can be a physical thing, like a car or a student, or an idea, like a course, a bank account or a loan. The key test is that we can point at it and say 'this one, not that one'.

Entity set: An entity set is a collection of entities of the same type, which share the same properties. All students form the entity set Student. All courses form the entity set Course. In an ER diagram an entity set is drawn as a rectangle with its name inside. Later, each entity set usually becomes a table, and each entity becomes a row. People often say entity when they mean entity set; the context makes it clear.

Attribute: An attribute is a property that describes an entity. A student has an id, a name, a date of birth, a phone number and a CGPA. Each attribute has a domain, the set of allowed values: CGPA's domain is numbers from 0.00 to 4.00, and phone numbers are strings of digits. In the classic Chen diagram, an attribute is drawn as an oval connected to its rectangle by a line.

Simple and composite attributes: A simple, or atomic, attribute cannot be split into smaller meaningful parts, like CGPA or roll number. A composite attribute is made of smaller parts. Name can be split into first name and last name. Address can be split into house, road, area, city and postcode, like 'House 12, Road 5, Dhanmondi, Dhaka 1205'. Composite attributes are drawn as an oval with its own smaller ovals branching off. Whether to treat something as composite depends on use: if the post office needs to sort letters by postcode, you should split the address.

Single-valued and multi-valued attributes: A single-valued attribute has one value per entity: each student has one date of birth. A multi-valued attribute can have several values for one entity: a student may have two or three phone numbers, or several email addresses. Multi-valued attributes are drawn as a double oval. As you will see in lesson 4, they need special care when we turn the diagram into tables, because a table cell should hold only one value.

Stored and derived attributes: A stored attribute is actually saved in the database, like date of birth. A derived attribute can be calculated from other data, like age, which comes from date of birth and today's date. It is wiser to store date of birth and calculate age when needed, because age changes every year while date of birth never does. A derived attribute is drawn as a dashed oval. CGPA can also be seen as derived, calculated from grades and credits, but many systems store it for speed.

Key attribute: A key attribute is an attribute whose value is different for every entity in the set, so it identifies each entity uniquely. Student id is a key: no two students share an id. Name is not a key, because two students can both be called Rahim. In the diagram, the key attribute's name is underlined. Sometimes a key needs more than one attribute together, like building plus room number for a classroom: Room 301 exists in many buildings, but 'Building A, Room 301' is unique.

NULL values: Sometimes an attribute has no value for an entity. A new student has no CGPA yet. A person without a landline has no landline number. Databases mark such cases as NULL, which means unknown or not applicable. NULL is not zero and not an empty string; it means there is nothing there. A CGPA of 0.00 and a NULL CGPA mean very different things, and lesson 8 shows how SQL handles NULL carefully.

Relationship: A relationship is an association between entities. Rina enrolls in CSE101. Dr. Karim teaches Data Structures. Sami belongs to the CSE department. A relationship set is a collection of similar relationships, like all the enrollments together. In a Chen diagram, a relationship set is drawn as a diamond, connected by lines to the entity sets it links. The name is usually a verb: Enrolls, Teaches, BelongsTo.

Relationship attributes: A relationship can have its own attributes. The grade Rina gets is not a property of Rina alone, because she has different grades in different courses. It is not a property of CSE101 alone either, because different students get different grades. The grade belongs to the pair: Rina in CSE101. So grade is an attribute of the Enrolls relationship, drawn as an oval attached to the diamond. Spotting attributes that belong to relationships is a sign of a good designer.

Degree of a relationship: The degree is the number of entity sets taking part. A binary relationship links two entity sets, like Student and Course in Enrolls; most relationships are binary. A ternary relationship links three, like Supplier supplies Part to Project, where we need to know all three together. A unary or recursive relationship links an entity set to itself, like Employee supervises Employee, or Course is a prerequisite of Course. In a recursive relationship, each side gets a role name, such as supervisor and supervisee, so we know who is who.

Cardinality ratios: The cardinality ratio says how many entities on one side can be linked to how many on the other. One-to-one, 1:1: each department has one head, and each teacher heads at most one department. One-to-many, 1:N: one department has many students, but each student belongs to one department. Many-to-one, N:1, is the same thing seen from the other side. Many-to-many, M:N: a student takes many courses, and a course has many students. The ratio is written next to the lines in the diagram, such as 1 and N, or M and N.

Reading cardinality the right way: To decide the ratio, ask two questions, one from each side. For one student, how many departments? One. For one department, how many students? Many. So Student to Department is N:1. For one student, how many courses? Many. For one course, how many students? Many. So Enrolls is M:N. Always ask both questions; asking only one gives wrong answers, and that is one of the most common mistakes in exams.

Participation constraints: Participation says whether every entity must take part in the relationship. Total participation means every entity must be linked: every student must belong to some department, so Student has total participation in BelongsTo. It is drawn as a double line. Partial participation means some entities may not be linked: not every teacher heads a department, so Teacher has partial participation in Heads, drawn as a single line. Cardinality and participation together are called structural constraints.

Min-max notation: Some books write each side as a pair (min, max). Student in BelongsTo is (1,1): at least one and at most one department. Department in BelongsTo is (0,N) if a new department might have no students yet, or (1,N) if every department must have at least one. A min of 0 means partial participation and a min of 1 or more means total participation. Watch out: different books place these labels on different sides of the diamond, so always read the legend of the notation your teacher uses.

A worked example, the university: Entity sets: Student (id, name, dob, phone multi-valued, age derived), Department (dept_id, name, building), Course (code, title, credits), Teacher (tid, name, designation). Relationships: BelongsTo between Student and Department, N:1, total on Student's side. Offers between Department and Course, 1:N, total on Course's side. Enrolls between Student and Course, M:N, with attribute grade. Teaches between Teacher and Course, M:N. Heads between Teacher and Department, 1:1, partial on Teacher's side, total on Department's side if every department must have a head. This one diagram already describes most of a university's data.

Crow's foot notation: In industry tools, you will often see crow's foot notation instead of Chen's. Entity sets are boxes listing their attributes inside, and relationships are just lines. The end of a line shows cardinality: a single bar means one, a three-pronged crow's foot means many, and a small circle means zero, which shows optional participation. The ideas are identical; only the drawing style changes. UML class diagrams are another style used by software engineers.

Real-life example 1, a Pathao-like ride app: Entity sets: Rider (rider_id, name, phone), Driver (driver_id, name, licence_no), Vehicle (plate_no, type), Trip (trip_id, pickup, drop, fare, time). Relationships: Rider requests Trip, 1:N, because one rider takes many trips but each trip has one rider. Driver drives Vehicle, which might be 1:1 in a simple design. Driver completes Trip, 1:N. Fare and time are attributes of Trip itself. Drawing this before coding makes the developers agree on details, such as whether one driver can use two vehicles.

Real-life example 2, a hospital: Patients, doctors, wards and appointments. A doctor sees many patients and a patient may see many doctors, so Sees is M:N, with attributes date and prescription on the relationship. A patient is admitted to one ward at a time, and a ward holds many patients, so AdmittedTo is N:1, with partial participation for patients because outdoor patients are never admitted. A doctor heads one ward at most, and each ward has exactly one head doctor: 1:1. Each of these decisions comes from asking the hospital how it really works.

Common mistakes and exam favourites: Making an attribute into an entity or the other way round. If something has its own attributes and links to other things, like Department, it should be an entity, not just a text attribute of Student. Putting grade on Student instead of on Enrolls. Forgetting to underline keys. Asking the cardinality question from only one side. Mixing up total participation, which is about whether every entity must take part, with cardinality, which is about how many. Exams often give a paragraph describing a company and ask you to draw the ER diagram with keys, cardinalities and participation.

Recap: An entity is a distinguishable thing, and an entity set is a group of similar entities, drawn as a rectangle. Attributes can be simple or composite, single- or multi-valued, stored or derived, and a key attribute identifies each entity. Relationships link entities, can have their own attributes, and have a degree. Cardinality ratios are 1:1, 1:N and M:N, and participation is total or partial. Next lesson adds weak entities, specialization and aggregation, and shows how to convert any ER diagram into tables.
key_points: The ER model, proposed by Peter Chen in 1976, describes data as entities, attributes and relationships before any tables are built.
An entity set is drawn as a rectangle, an attribute as an oval and a relationship set as a diamond.
Attributes can be simple or composite, single-valued or multi-valued (double oval), stored or derived (dashed oval); keys are underlined.
A relationship can have its own attributes, such as grade on Enrolls between Student and Course.
Degree counts the entity sets in a relationship: unary (recursive), binary or ternary.
Cardinality ratios are 1:1, 1:N and M:N; always ask the 'how many' question from both sides.
Total participation (double line) means every entity must take part; partial (single line) means some may not.
lessons.tip: For any ER problem, first underline the nouns in the question (entity or attribute candidates) and circle the verbs (relationship candidates). Then for every relationship, write the two 'for one X, how many Y?' questions before drawing a single line.
lessons.task: Draw an ER diagram for your neighbourhood library: Member, Book, Author and Loan. Decide the keys, find one composite attribute and one multi-valued attribute, mark the cardinality of 'Member borrows Book' and 'Author writes Book', and decide where the attribute 'due date' belongs.

quiz.q: A student can have several phone numbers. In an ER diagram, phone is best shown as:
quiz.explain: One entity having several values for the same property is a multi-valued attribute, drawn as a double oval.

quiz.q: Where does the attribute 'grade' belong in the university design?
options: On the Enrolls relationship between Student and Course
quiz.explain: A grade depends on both the student and the course together, so it is an attribute of the Enrolls relationship.

quiz.q: Each student belongs to exactly one department, and a department has many students. The cardinality of Student to Department is:
quiz.explain: Many students map to one department, so from Student's side it is many-to-one (N:1).

quiz.q: 'Employee supervises Employee' is an example of a:
quiz.explain: The same entity set appears on both sides with different roles (supervisor and supervisee), so it is recursive or unary.

quiz.q: Age is calculated from date of birth. In the ER model, age is a:
quiz.explain: An attribute whose value can be computed from other stored data is derived, drawn as a dashed oval.

lessons.title: The ER Model II: Weak Entities, Specialization, Aggregation and Mapping to Tables
lessons.content:
Think about the rooms of a flat in a building in Uttara. 'Flat 4B' means nothing on its own, because almost every building has a Flat 4B. It only makes sense together with the building: 'Flat 4B of Building 7, Road 12'. Some things in data are exactly like that: they cannot be identified without their owner. In this lesson you will meet such weak entities, learn how to show family trees of entity types with specialization and generalization, learn aggregation, and finally learn the step-by-step recipe that turns any ER diagram into real tables.

Strong and weak entity sets: A strong entity set has its own key. Student has id, Course has code. A weak entity set does not have enough attributes to form a key by itself. Its entities can only be identified by being linked to an entity of another set, called the owner or identifying entity set. The relationship that links them is the identifying relationship. A weak entity always has total participation in this relationship, because a weak entity without its owner cannot exist.

A classic weak entity, dependents: A company stores its employees' dependents, such as children, for medical insurance. A dependent has a name, date of birth and relation. Two different employees can both have a son named Arif. So dependent name alone is not unique. But within one employee's family, names are unique. Dependent is a weak entity, Employee is its owner, and the identifying relationship is HasDependent. The dependent's name is its partial key, also called the discriminator: it is unique only inside one owner.

Drawing weak entities: In a Chen diagram, a weak entity set is drawn as a double rectangle, its identifying relationship as a double diamond, and its partial key is underlined with a dashed line. The full key of a dependent is the owner's key plus the partial key: (employee_id, dependent_name). Another common example is Section of a Course: section 1, section 2 and section 3 exist for many courses, but 'CSE101 section 2' is unique. Installments of a loan, rooms of a building and order lines of an order are also weak entities.

Weak or just a foreign key: Not every dependent-looking thing must be weak. If you give each section a global id like 5021, Section becomes a strong entity. Designers choose weak entities when the real world identifies them through the owner, and when deleting the owner should delete them too. If an employee leaves and is deleted, his dependents should disappear with him, which matches the idea of a weak entity.

Specialization: Sometimes one entity set has subgroups with extra attributes. All university persons have id, name and phone. But students also have CGPA and teachers also have salary and designation. Specialization is the top-down process of defining subclasses, Student and Teacher, under a superclass, Person. Each subclass inherits all attributes and relationships of the superclass and adds its own. In the diagram, a triangle or a circle labelled ISA connects the superclass to its subclasses.

Generalization: Generalization is the same picture built bottom-up. You notice that Car and Bike both have plate number, owner and tax token date, so you pull the common attributes into a superclass, Vehicle. Specialization starts from the general and finds differences; generalization starts from the specific and finds common parts. The final diagram looks the same, which is why books often treat them together.

Constraints on specialization: Disjointness asks: can an entity belong to more than one subclass? Disjoint means at most one: a vehicle is either a car or a bike, not both. Overlapping means it can be in several: a person at a university can be both a student and a teacher, like a lecturer doing a master's degree. Completeness asks: must every superclass entity belong to some subclass? Total specialization means yes: every account is either savings or current. Partial specialization means no: some persons may be neither student nor teacher, such as guards or visitors. These two constraints combine into four possible cases.

Aggregation: The ER model cannot normally draw a relationship to another relationship. But sometimes we need to. Say students work on projects, a relationship WorksOn between Student and Project. A teacher monitors each student-project pair, not just the student or just the project. Aggregation treats the whole WorksOn relationship, with its entity sets, as one higher-level entity, drawn with a box around it. Then a new relationship, Monitors, can connect Teacher to that box. Aggregation keeps the design honest without inventing fake entities.

Design choices: The same world can be drawn in more than one way, and the choice matters. Entity or attribute? If a department only needs a name, an attribute of Student might do; but once it has a building, a head and courses, it must be an entity. Entity or relationship? A loan between a bank and a customer could be a relationship, but if loans have payments, numbers and dates of their own, a Loan entity is better. Binary or ternary? If a supplier supplies parts and also works on projects, two binary relationships say less than one ternary Supplies relationship, which records exactly which part went to which project. Good designers ask what questions the database must answer, then pick the drawing that answers them without duplication.

The mapping recipe, step 1, strong entities: For each strong entity set, make a table. Its columns are the simple attributes. For a composite attribute, keep only its parts: address becomes house, road, area, city. Skip derived attributes, since they can be calculated. Choose the key as the primary key. So Student(id, name, dob) and Department(dept_id, name, building). Multi-valued attributes are handled separately in step 6.

Step 2, weak entities: For each weak entity set, make a table with its own attributes plus the primary key of the owner as a foreign key. The primary key is the owner's key plus the partial key. Dependent(employee_id, dep_name, dob, relation), with primary key (employee_id, dep_name) and employee_id pointing to Employee. Usually we also set ON DELETE CASCADE, so deleting the employee deletes the dependents, matching their weak nature.

Step 3, one-to-one relationships: Pick one side, preferably the side with total participation, and add the other side's key as a foreign key. For Teacher heads Department, 1:1, with total participation on Department's side, add head_tid to Department. Any attributes of the relationship, like start_date, go there too. Putting the key on the total side avoids lots of NULL values. Another option, if both sides are total, is to merge the two tables into one.

Step 4, one-to-many relationships: Put the key of the one side as a foreign key in the table of the many side. Each student belongs to one department, so add dept_id to Student: Student(id, name, dob, dept_id). Relationship attributes also go to the many side. Never do it the other way round: putting a list of student ids inside Department would need many values in one cell, which tables do not allow.

Step 5, many-to-many relationships: Make a new table for the relationship. Its columns are the primary keys of both sides, as foreign keys, plus the relationship's own attributes. Its primary key is usually the combination of both foreign keys. Enrolls becomes Enroll(student_id, course_code, grade), with primary key (student_id, course_code). This table is often called a junction, bridge or associative table. Each row says one fact: this student took this course and got this grade.

Step 6, multi-valued attributes: Make a new table with the entity's key plus the attribute. Student phones become StudentPhone(student_id, phone), with primary key (student_id, phone). Rina with two numbers gets two rows. This keeps every cell holding a single value, which lesson 14 will call first normal form.

Step 7, n-ary relationships: For a ternary relationship like Supplies(Supplier, Part, Project, quantity), make a table with all three keys as foreign keys plus quantity. The primary key is usually all three keys together, unless a cardinality of 1 on some side allows a smaller key. A ternary relationship cannot always be replaced by three binary ones without losing information, which is why it is mapped as one table.

Step 8, specialization: There are three common options. One: a table for the superclass and one table for each subclass, where each subclass table has the superclass key as both its primary key and a foreign key: Person(id, name, phone), Student(id, cgpa), Teacher(id, salary, designation). This works for every case. Two: only subclass tables, each copying all superclass attributes: Student(id, name, phone, cgpa). This works well for disjoint and total specialization. Three: one big table with all attributes and a type column, filling NULL where an attribute does not apply. It is fast to query but wastes space when subclasses differ a lot.

A full worked mapping: From last lesson's university diagram we get: Department(dept_id, name, building, head_tid), Teacher(tid, name, designation), Student(id, name, dob, dept_id), StudentPhone(student_id, phone), Course(code, title, credits, dept_id), Enroll(student_id, course_code, grade), Teaches(tid, course_code). Seven tables. Check: every M:N became its own table, every 1:N became a foreign key on the many side, the derived age disappeared, the multi-valued phone got its own table. That is exactly the schema used in the SQL lessons ahead, slightly simplified.

Real-life example 1, a bank: Account is specialized into SavingsAccount, with interest rate, and CurrentAccount, with overdraft limit, disjoint and total. Loan payments are a weak entity of Loan, identified by (loan_no, payment_no). Customer owns Account is M:N, because joint accounts exist, so it becomes a table Owns(customer_id, account_no). Mapping this correctly matters a lot: a wrong design could, for example, stop a joint account holder from seeing his own account.

Real-life example 2, an online exam system: Question is generalized from MCQ, with options, and Written, with marks for each part. An attempt is an M:N relationship between Student and Exam. A teacher checks each attempt, which needs aggregation: Checks connects Teacher to the Student-Exam attempt. During mapping, the attempt becomes Attempt(student_id, exam_id, start_time) and Checks becomes a foreign key checker_tid in Attempt, because each attempt is checked by one teacher.

Common mistakes and exam favourites: Giving a weak entity a fake key instead of using the owner's key plus the partial key. Putting the foreign key on the one side of a 1:N relationship. Forgetting to make a separate table for an M:N relationship. Storing multi-valued attributes as comma-separated text like '017..., 018...'. Mixing up disjoint/overlapping with total/partial. Exams love asking: define weak entity with an example, explain specialization vs generalization, explain aggregation with a diagram, and convert a given ER diagram into a relational schema with keys marked.

Recap: Weak entities depend on an owner and are identified by the owner's key plus a partial key; they are drawn with double rectangles and double diamonds. Specialization and generalization build class hierarchies, with disjoint or overlapping and total or partial constraints. Aggregation treats a relationship as an entity. Mapping turns strong entities into tables, weak entities into tables with the owner's key, 1:1 and 1:N relationships into foreign keys, M:N relationships and multi-valued attributes into new tables, and specializations into one of three table patterns. Next you will study tables themselves: the relational model.
key_points: A weak entity set has no key of its own; it is identified by its owner's key plus a partial key, and always has total participation in the identifying relationship.
Weak entities use double rectangles, identifying relationships use double diamonds, partial keys get a dashed underline.
Specialization (top-down) and generalization (bottom-up) create superclass and subclass hierarchies with inheritance.
Specialization constraints: disjoint or overlapping, and total or partial.
Aggregation treats a relationship and its entities as one higher-level entity so another relationship can link to it.
Mapping: 1:N puts the one side's key into the many side; M:N and multi-valued attributes become new tables.
Specialization can map to superclass plus subclass tables, subclass tables only, or one table with a type column.
lessons.tip: After mapping any ER diagram, do a quick self-check: count the M:N relationships and multi-valued attributes, and make sure each became its own table. Then make sure no cell would ever need to hold a list. If both checks pass, your mapping is almost certainly right.
lessons.task: Take the library ER diagram from the last lesson's task and map it to tables on paper. Mark every primary key with an underline and every foreign key with an arrow to the table it points to. Then add a weak entity, 'Copy' of a book (copy 1, copy 2 of the same title), and map it too.

quiz.q: What is the primary key of a weak entity table such as Dependent?
options: The owner's primary key plus the weak entity's partial key
The weak entity has no primary key
quiz.explain: A weak entity is identified through its owner, so its key combines the owner's key with its own partial key (discriminator).

quiz.q: Each student belongs to one department; a department has many students. How is this mapped?
options: A list of student ids stored in Department
dept_id added as a foreign key in Student
id added as a foreign key in Department
quiz.explain: For 1:N, the key of the one side (Department) goes into the table of the many side (Student).

quiz.q: A person at a university can be both a student and a teacher at the same time. This specialization is:
quiz.explain: Overlapping means an entity may belong to more than one subclass at once.

quiz.q: Why is aggregation used?
options: To combine two tables into one
To let a relationship connect to another relationship treated as an entity
quiz.explain: Aggregation wraps a relationship and its entities into a higher-level entity so that a new relationship can link to it.

quiz.q: How should the multi-valued attribute 'phone' of Student be mapped?
options: As a comma-separated text column in Student
As three columns phone1, phone2, phone3
As a new table StudentPhone(student_id, phone)
quiz.explain: A separate table with the owner's key and the value keeps every cell single-valued and allows any number of phones.

lessons.title: The Relational Model: Tables, Keys and Integrity Constraints
lessons.content:
Open the class register your teacher carries. Each row is one student, each column is one piece of information: roll, name, father's name, phone. Nobody needs a manual to read it. That simple idea, store everything as tables, is the relational model, and in 1970 Edgar Codd showed that it could be made mathematically precise. Almost every database you will meet, from bKash's accounts to your university's results, stores its data this way. This lesson gives you the exact vocabulary and the rules that keep tables trustworthy.

Relation means table: In the relational model, a table is called a relation. Each row is called a tuple, and each column is called an attribute. The name comes from mathematics: you met relations in discrete maths as sets of ordered pairs, and a table with n columns is just a set of n-tuples. So student(id, name, dept_id, cgpa, city) is a relation with five attributes, and (1, 'Rina', 'CSE', 3.80, 'Dhaka') is one tuple in it.

Formal words and everyday words: Relation is table, tuple is row or record, attribute is column or field. The relation schema is the name plus the list of attributes, like student(id, name, dept_id, cgpa, city). The relation instance is the set of tuples present right now. The degree, or arity, of a relation is its number of attributes; student has degree 5. The cardinality is the number of tuples; with five students, the cardinality is 5. Be careful: this cardinality is about counting rows and is different from the cardinality ratio of ER relationships.

Domains: Each attribute takes values from a domain, the set of allowed values. The domain of cgpa might be decimal numbers from 0.00 to 4.00. The domain of dept_id might be short codes like CSE, EEE and BBA. In the pure relational model every domain is atomic: a value cannot be split further inside the database. A cell holds one value, not a list and not a small table. This rule is the heart of first normal form, which you will study in lesson 14.

Properties of a relation: Because a relation is a set, it has some surprising properties. One, no two tuples are exactly the same; duplicates are not allowed in pure theory. Two, the order of tuples does not matter: the student table with Rina first or Sami first is the same relation. Three, the order of attributes does not matter either, as long as we refer to them by name. Four, every value is atomic. Real SQL databases relax some of these, for example SQL tables can contain duplicate rows unless you forbid them, but the theory keeps them strict.

Why keys: Since duplicates are not allowed, every tuple must be distinguishable from every other one. A key is a set of attributes whose values tell tuples apart. Keys are how one table points at another, how searches find exactly one record, and how the database blocks double entries, like admitting the same student twice. There are several kinds of keys, and the exam loves asking you to separate them.

Superkey: A superkey is any set of attributes whose values are unique for every tuple. In student, {id} is a superkey. {id, name} is also a superkey, because if id alone is unique, adding name keeps it unique. {id, name, city} is a superkey too. In fact, the set of all attributes is always a superkey, because no two tuples are completely identical. Superkeys can have extra, unnecessary attributes.

Candidate key: A candidate key is a minimal superkey: a superkey from which you cannot remove any attribute without losing uniqueness. {id} is a candidate key. {id, name} is not, because removing name still leaves a superkey. A relation can have several candidate keys. If every student also has a unique national ID number, nid, then {nid} is another candidate key. A candidate key can have more than one attribute: in enroll(student_id, course_code, grade), neither student_id nor course_code alone is unique, but together {student_id, course_code} is a candidate key.

Keys come from meaning, not from today's data: Look at a small instance where, by chance, all five students live in different cities. Is city a key? No. Today the values happen to differ, but tomorrow a second student from Dhaka will be admitted, and the rule must still hold. A key is a promise about every possible instance, so it is decided from the real-world meaning: the university guarantees that ids are never reused, but nobody guarantees that cities are unique. Looking at sample data can prove that something is not a key, if you see a repeated value, but it can never prove that something is a key. Exams sometimes test exactly this with a tiny table where a non-key column looks unique.

Primary key and alternate keys: From the candidate keys, the designer chooses one to be the primary key: the main way to identify rows. Usually we pick a short, stable one, like id rather than nid, because ids never change and are small to store. The other candidate keys are called alternate keys or secondary keys. The primary key is underlined in schema diagrams: student(id underlined, name, dept_id, cgpa, city).

Choosing a good primary key: A good primary key is unique, never NULL, short and never changes. Phone numbers are a bad choice: people change SIMs. Names are terrible: duplicates. Email can change. So many systems invent a surrogate key, a meaningless number like 1, 2, 3 handed out by the database, instead of a natural key that comes from the real world. Your student id, your bKash transaction id and your Daraz order number are all surrogate-style keys.

Foreign key: A foreign key is an attribute, or set of attributes, in one relation that refers to the primary key of another relation, or of the same one. In student, dept_id is a foreign key referring to department(dept_id). It means: the value in student.dept_id must be a department that actually exists. The table holding the foreign key is called the referencing or child table; the table it points to is called the referenced or parent table. Foreign keys are the threads that tie tables together, and they are how 1:N and M:N relationships from the ER diagram live in tables.

A self-referencing foreign key: A foreign key can point to its own table. In employee(emp_id, name, supervisor_id), supervisor_id refers to emp_id of the same table. Rahim's supervisor_id is 7, meaning employee 7 is his boss. The big boss has supervisor_id NULL. This is how the recursive relationship from lesson 3 is stored.

NULL and keys: NULL means unknown or not applicable. A foreign key may be NULL if the relationship is optional: a new student who has not chosen a department yet might have dept_id NULL, if the design allows it. But a primary key may never be NULL, because then we could not identify the row. That leads to the integrity constraints.

Domain constraint: Every value must come from its attribute's domain. A cgpa of 5.2 or 'abc' breaks the domain constraint. In SQL this is enforced by the data type and by CHECK rules, such as CHECK (cgpa BETWEEN 0 AND 4). A NOT NULL rule is also a kind of domain constraint, saying that NULL is not in the allowed set.

Key and entity integrity constraints: The key constraint says no two tuples may have the same value for a candidate key. The entity integrity constraint says no primary key value may be NULL. Together they guarantee that every row can be found and identified exactly. If someone tries to insert a second student with id 1, or a student with id NULL, the DBMS refuses.

Referential integrity constraint: This says every non-NULL foreign key value must match an existing primary key value in the referenced table. If the department table has CSE, EEE and BBA, then inserting a student with dept_id 'MATH' is rejected. Referential integrity prevents 'orphans', child rows pointing to parents that do not exist, like an enrollment for a student who was never admitted.

What happens on delete or update: Suppose someone deletes the EEE department while Tuli's row still says dept_id = 'EEE'. The DBMS must do something. The options, written in SQL as ON DELETE actions, are: RESTRICT or NO ACTION, which refuses the delete while children exist; CASCADE, which deletes the children too; SET NULL, which sets the children's foreign key to NULL; and SET DEFAULT, which sets it to a default value. The same choices exist ON UPDATE, if a parent's key value changes. CASCADE is good for weak entities like order lines; RESTRICT is safer for important data like student records.

A worked check: Take department {CSE, EEE, BBA} and student rows (1, Rina, CSE), (2, Sami, CSE), (3, Tuli, EEE). Which of these operations violate a constraint? Insert (2, Mitu, BBA): violates the key constraint, id 2 exists. Insert (NULL, Mitu, BBA): violates entity integrity. Insert (6, Mitu, ARCH): violates referential integrity, ARCH is not a department. Delete department CSE with RESTRICT: rejected, because Rina and Sami refer to it. Delete department BBA: allowed, because no student refers to it in this instance. Update Tuli's dept_id to BBA: allowed.

Real-life example 1, a bKash-style wallet: The account table has primary key account_no. The transaction table has txn_id as its primary key and two foreign keys, from_account and to_account, both referencing account. Referential integrity guarantees that money can never be sent to an account number that does not exist in the system. A CHECK constraint can make sure amount is greater than zero. And because txn_id is unique, the same transaction cannot be recorded twice, which matters when customers complain.

Real-life example 2, a Daraz order: orders(order_id, customer_id, order_date) and order_item(order_id, line_no, product_id, quantity). order_item's primary key is (order_id, line_no), a composite key, and order_id is also a foreign key with ON DELETE CASCADE: if an unpaid order is deleted, its lines vanish too. product_id references product with ON DELETE RESTRICT, so a product that appears in past orders cannot be deleted by mistake; instead it is marked as discontinued.

Common mistakes and exam favourites: Mixing up superkey and candidate key: every candidate key is a superkey, but not every superkey is a candidate key. Thinking the primary key must be a single column: it can be composite. Thinking a foreign key must be unique: it is not; many students share dept_id 'CSE'. Thinking a foreign key cannot be NULL: it can, unless NOT NULL is added. Using degree and cardinality the wrong way round. Common questions: define all the key types with one example table, list the integrity constraints, and decide which given insert or delete operations violate which constraint.

Recap: A relation is a table of tuples and attributes, with degree as its number of columns and cardinality as its number of rows. Values are atomic and come from domains. Superkeys identify tuples, candidate keys are minimal superkeys, one becomes the primary key and the rest are alternate keys. Foreign keys reference primary keys and tie tables together. The domain, key, entity integrity and referential integrity constraints keep data correct, and ON DELETE and ON UPDATE actions decide what happens to children. Next lesson, you will learn the algebra used to ask questions of these tables.
key_points: A relation is a table: tuples are rows, attributes are columns; degree is the number of attributes, cardinality the number of tuples.
Values are atomic and come from the attribute's domain; tuple order and attribute order do not matter in theory.
A superkey uniquely identifies tuples; a candidate key is a minimal superkey; the chosen one is the primary key, the rest are alternate keys.
A foreign key refers to a primary key in another (or the same) table; it can repeat and can be NULL unless forbidden.
Entity integrity: a primary key is never NULL. Referential integrity: every non-NULL foreign key matches an existing primary key.
ON DELETE / ON UPDATE actions are RESTRICT/NO ACTION, CASCADE, SET NULL and SET DEFAULT.
Good primary keys are unique, non-NULL, short and stable; surrogate keys are often used for this.
lessons.tip: For every table you design, say aloud: 'one row of this table means one ...'. If you can finish the sentence ('one enrollment of one student in one course'), the primary key usually becomes obvious from that sentence.
lessons.task: Write the tables student, department and enroll from this lesson on paper with three or four rows each. Then invent five operations (two inserts, two deletes, one update) and, for each, write whether it is allowed or which constraint it violates. Try one delete with CASCADE and see which rows disappear.

quiz.q: In enroll(student_id, course_code, grade), a student can take many courses and a course has many students. What is a candidate key?
quiz.explain: Neither column alone is unique, but each student-course pair appears once, so the pair together is a minimal superkey.

quiz.q: A relation has 6 attributes and 250 tuples. What are its degree and cardinality?
quiz.explain: Degree counts attributes (columns) and cardinality counts tuples (rows).

quiz.q: Inserting a student with dept_id 'MATH' when no MATH department exists violates:
quiz.explain: A non-NULL foreign key value must match an existing primary key in the referenced table; MATH does not exist.

quiz.q: Which statement about foreign keys is true?
options: A foreign key value may repeat in many rows
A foreign key must be unique in its table
A foreign key can never be NULL
A foreign key must be the primary key of its own table
quiz.explain: Many students can share dept_id 'CSE'. Foreign keys are not required to be unique, and they can be NULL unless NOT NULL is added.

quiz.q: Which ON DELETE action removes the child rows when the parent row is deleted?
quiz.explain: CASCADE spreads the delete to the referencing rows; RESTRICT and NO ACTION refuse it, and SET NULL keeps the children with a NULL key.

lessons.title: Relational Algebra: The Maths of Asking Questions
lessons.content:
When you do arithmetic, you take numbers and apply operations like plus and times to get new numbers. Relational algebra is the same game, but with tables. You take tables, apply operations like 'pick rows' or 'pick columns' or 'join', and get new tables. Every question you ask a relational database, no matter how complicated, can be broken into a few of these simple operations. Inside every DBMS, your SQL query is turned into a tree of exactly these operations before it runs. Learn them well, and both SQL and query optimization will feel natural.

The running data: We use four tables. student(id, name, dept_id, cgpa, city) has Rina (CSE, 3.80, Dhaka), Sami (CSE, 3.20, Chattogram), Tuli (EEE, 3.55, Sylhet), Upol (BBA, 2.90, Dhaka) and Nadia (CSE, CGPA not yet known, Khulna), with ids 1 to 5. department(dept_id, name, building) has CSE in Building A, EEE in Building B and BBA in Building C. course(code, title, credits, dept_id) has CSE101, CSE201, EEE101 and BBA101. enroll(student_id, course_code, grade) has six rows: Rina in CSE101 and CSE201, Sami in CSE101, Tuli in EEE101 and CSE101, and Upol in BBA101. Nadia has no enrollments yet.

Closure, the key idea: Every operation takes one or two relations and returns a relation. Because the output is again a table, you can feed it into another operation, like chaining plus and times in arithmetic. This property is called closure, and it is why complex queries can be built from small pieces. The basic operations are selection, projection, union, set difference, Cartesian product and rename. The others, like joins, intersection and division, can be built from these six.

Selection, sigma: Selection picks the rows that satisfy a condition. It is written with the Greek letter sigma: sigma with condition cgpa > 3.5, applied to student. The result has the same columns as student but only the rows that pass the test: Rina and Tuli. Nadia does not appear, because her CGPA is unknown and an unknown value cannot be shown to be greater than 3.5. Conditions can use comparisons like =, <, >, not equal, and combine them with AND, OR and NOT, like dept_id = 'CSE' AND city = 'Dhaka', which gives only Rina. Think of selection as a horizontal cut through the table.

Projection, pi: Projection picks columns and throws the rest away. It is written with pi: pi of name, cgpa applied to student gives a two-column table. Projection is a vertical cut. Because a relation is a set, projection removes duplicate rows. Pi of city on student gives Dhaka, Chattogram, Sylhet and Khulna: four rows, not five, because Rina and Upol both live in Dhaka. This duplicate removal is one of the differences between pure algebra and SQL, which keeps duplicates unless you write DISTINCT.

Combining selection and projection: 'Names of CSE students' is pi of name applied to sigma of dept_id = 'CSE' applied to student. Read it from the inside out: first keep the CSE rows, then keep only the name column. The answer is Rina, Sami and Nadia. You could also write it as a sequence of steps with temporary names: T1 gets sigma dept_id = 'CSE' (student), then the answer is pi name (T1). Both forms are correct; the step form is easier to read in long answers.

Union, intersection and difference: These are the usual set operations, and they need union-compatible relations: the same number of columns, with matching domains. Let A be the ids of students in CSE101: {1, 2, 3}. Let B be the ids of students in EEE101: {3}. A union B gives {1, 2, 3}: students in either course. A intersect B gives {3}: Tuli, the only student in both. A minus B gives {1, 2}: students in CSE101 but not EEE101. Difference is not symmetric: B minus A is empty. Intersection is not basic, because A intersect B equals A minus (A minus B).

Cartesian product, times: The Cartesian product, also called cross product, pairs every row of one table with every row of another. student times department has 5 times 3 = 15 rows and 5 + 3 = 8 columns. Most of these pairs are nonsense, like Rina paired with the EEE department. The product is rarely useful alone, but followed by a selection like student.dept_id = department.dept_id, it keeps only the matching pairs. That combination is so common that it gets its own name: join.

Rename, rho: Rename, written with the Greek letter rho, gives a relation or its attributes a new name. It is needed when you combine a table with itself. To find pairs of students from the same city, you need two copies of student, say S1 and S2, and then select S1.city = S2.city AND S1.id < S2.id. Without renaming, the two copies would have identical attribute names and you could not tell them apart. The answer is the single pair Rina and Upol, both from Dhaka.

Theta join and equi-join: A theta join is a Cartesian product followed by a selection with any condition theta. When the condition only uses equality, like student.dept_id = department.dept_id, it is called an equi-join. The result still has both dept_id columns, which contain identical values in every row.

Natural join, the bow-tie symbol: The natural join joins two tables on all attributes with the same name, keeps only rows where those attributes are equal, and keeps just one copy of each common column. student natural join department matches on dept_id and gives five rows, each student with the department's name and building. Natural join is powerful but risky: if two tables accidentally share a column name, like name in both student and department, the natural join would also require student name to equal department name, giving an empty result. Always check which columns are shared.

Outer joins: An ordinary join drops rows that have no partner. student joined with enroll on id equals student_id loses Nadia, because she has no enrollment. A left outer join keeps every row of the left table and fills the missing right side with NULL. student left outer join enroll gives seven rows: six real matches plus Nadia with NULL course and NULL grade. A right outer join keeps every row of the right table, and a full outer join keeps unmatched rows of both. Outer joins are how you answer 'show all students, even those with no courses'.

Division: Division answers 'for all' questions. 'Which students have taken all CSE courses?' Let R be pi of student_id and course_code from enroll, and S be pi of code, renamed course_code, from sigma dept_id = 'CSE' (course), which is {CSE101, CSE201}. R divided by S gives the student ids that are paired in R with every course in S. Rina has both, Sami and Tuli have only CSE101, so the answer is {1}, Rina. Division can be written with the basic operations, but the expression is long, so the symbol saves effort.

Assignment and query trees: For long queries we use temporary relations with an arrow, like T1 gets sigma dept_id = 'CSE' (student). A DBMS represents the same thing as a query tree: leaves are tables, inner nodes are operations, and data flows from the leaves up to the root. For example: names and buildings of students with CGPA above 3.5 is pi name, building (sigma cgpa > 3.5 (student natural join department)). The tree has student and department at the bottom, a join above them, then the selection, then the projection at the top. The answer is Rina in Building A and Tuli in Building B.

Equivalent expressions: Many different expressions give the same answer. pi name, building (sigma cgpa > 3.5 (student natural join department)) gives the same result as pi name, building ((sigma cgpa > 3.5 (student)) natural join department). The second one is usually cheaper, because it shrinks student to two rows before joining. This is the seed of query optimization: rewrite the tree into an equivalent but cheaper one. Lesson 19 builds on exactly this idea.

Extended operations: Real systems add a few more operations. Generalized projection allows calculations, like pi of name and cgpa times 25 to show a percentage-like score. Aggregation, written with a script G, computes things like count, sum and average per group: dept_id G count(id) (student) gives CSE 3, EEE 1, BBA 1. These match SQL's GROUP BY, which you will see in lesson 9.

Relational calculus, a peek: Algebra is procedural: you say which operations to apply, in what order. Relational calculus is declarative: you describe what the answer looks like and let the system find it. In tuple relational calculus, 'names of CSE students' is written as the set of t.name such that t is in student and t.dept_id = 'CSE'. Domain relational calculus does the same with variables for single values instead of whole tuples. Codd proved that relational algebra and safe relational calculus have the same power. A language that can express every query of the algebra is called relationally complete, and SQL is relationally complete.

Real-life example 1, a Daraz filter: You search for 'phone' with filters 'under 20,000 taka' and 'seller in Dhaka'. Behind the scenes this is a selection on product with price < 20000, a join with seller on seller_id, another selection on seller city, and a projection on the columns shown in the list: name, price and rating. If you sort and show only the first page, extra steps are added on top, but the core is pure relational algebra.

Real-life example 2, a scholarship list: A university wants students who passed every course they took in the first year and have CGPA at least 3.5. One way: T1 is the ids of students with any F grade in first-year courses; T2 is the ids of students with cgpa >= 3.5; the answer is T2 minus T1, joined with student to get names. Difference is the natural tool for 'no failure' conditions, and the officer who writes the SQL is really writing this algebra.

Common mistakes and exam favourites: Forgetting that projection removes duplicates in algebra. Using union on relations that are not union-compatible. Using natural join between tables that share an extra column name by accident. Forgetting the rename when joining a table with itself. Mixing up the order in division. Writing a Cartesian product with no selection and getting a huge wrong answer.
