Typical exam questions give a schema and ask for five to ten queries in relational algebra, ask you to evaluate an expression on small tables, or ask you to explain division with an example.

Recap: Relational algebra has six basic operations: selection picks rows, projection picks columns, union and difference combine union-compatible tables, Cartesian product pairs all rows, and rename gives new names. Joins, intersection and division are built from them. Outer joins keep unmatched rows with NULLs. Equivalent expressions can have very different costs, which is the basis of optimization. Relational calculus describes answers instead of steps and has the same power. Next lesson, you will write real SQL, starting with how to create tables and put data in them.
key_points: Relational algebra operations take relations and return relations (closure), so they can be chained into query trees.
Basic operations: selection (sigma, rows), projection (pi, columns), union, set difference, Cartesian product and rename (rho).
Projection removes duplicates in pure algebra; union, intersection and difference need union-compatible relations.
A join is a Cartesian product followed by a selection; natural join matches all same-named columns and keeps one copy.
Outer joins (left, right, full) keep unmatched rows and fill the missing side with NULL.
Division answers 'for all' questions, like students who took all CSE courses.
Equivalent expressions can differ greatly in cost, which is the starting point of query optimization.
lessons.tip: Practise algebra with tiny tables of three to five rows you can see on paper. Evaluate every expression by hand, row by row. Once you can predict results exactly, writing the same queries in SQL becomes almost mechanical.
lessons.task: Using the student, course and enroll rows in this lesson, write relational algebra for: (a) ids of students who took CSE101 but not CSE201, (b) names of students from Dhaka in CSE, (c) titles of courses Tuli has taken. Evaluate each by hand and write the answer tables.

quiz.q: student has 5 rows and 5 columns; department has 3 rows and 3 columns. How many rows and columns does student times department have?
quiz.explain: The Cartesian product pairs every row with every row (5 x 3 = 15) and puts all columns side by side (5 + 3 = 8).

quiz.q: In pure relational algebra, pi of city on student, where two students live in Dhaka, returns:
quiz.explain: A relation is a set, so projection removes duplicate rows; Dhaka appears once.

quiz.q: Which operation keeps all students, including those with no enrollments, when combined with enroll?
options: Left outer join (student on the left)
quiz.explain: A left outer join keeps every row from the left table and fills the missing right side with NULL.

quiz.q: 'Find students who have taken every CSE course' is best expressed with:
quiz.explain: Division returns the values paired with all values of the divisor, which is exactly a 'for all' question.

quiz.q: Why is the rename operation needed when finding pairs of students from the same city?
options: Because a table is joined with itself and the two copies need different names
Because projection removes the city column
quiz.explain: Joining student with itself needs two distinguishable copies (S1 and S2), which rename provides.

lessons.title: SQL I: Creating Tables and Changing Data
lessons.content:
Relational algebra is the maths; SQL is the language people actually type. If you work as a software engineer in Dhaka, in Bengaluru or in Berlin, you will write SQL, whether the company uses MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server or SQLite. The good news is that SQL reads almost like English: CREATE TABLE, INSERT INTO, UPDATE, DELETE FROM. In this lesson you will build the university database from scratch and learn how to put data in, change it and remove it, while the database guards its own rules.

Where SQL came from: In the early 1970s, IBM researchers Donald Chamberlin and Raymond Boyce designed a language called SEQUEL for IBM's experimental relational system, System R. The name was later shortened to SQL. Many people still say 'sequel', and others spell out S-Q-L; both are fine. SQL became an ANSI standard in 1986 and an ISO standard in 1987, and it has been updated many times since. Every product follows the standard mostly but adds its own small differences, called dialects. The core you learn here works almost everywhere.

The parts of SQL: SQL has a few sub-languages. DDL, data definition language, defines structure: CREATE, ALTER, DROP. DML, data manipulation language, works with rows: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE. DCL, data control language, handles permissions: GRANT and REVOKE. TCL, transaction control language, handles transactions: COMMIT, ROLLBACK and SAVEPOINT. Some books put SELECT in its own group called DQL, data query language. SQL keywords are not case-sensitive, so create table and CREATE TABLE are the same, but writing keywords in capitals makes code easier to read. Each statement ends with a semicolon.

Data types: Every column needs a type. Common ones: INT or INTEGER for whole numbers, like id or credits. DECIMAL(p, s) or NUMERIC(p, s) for exact decimals, where p is the total number of digits and s the digits after the point; DECIMAL(3,2) holds values like 3.80. Use DECIMAL for money, never floating point, because floats cannot store 0.1 exactly and small errors pile up. FLOAT and REAL are approximate numbers for science. CHAR(n) is a fixed-length string, padded with spaces; VARCHAR(n) is a variable-length string up to n characters. DATE, TIME and TIMESTAMP store dates and times. BOOLEAN stores true or false in many systems. TEXT or CLOB holds long text, and BLOB holds binary data like images.

Creating a table: Here is the department table. CREATE TABLE department (dept_id CHAR(5) PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(60) NOT NULL UNIQUE, building VARCHAR(20)); Each column has a name and a type, then optional constraints. PRIMARY KEY makes dept_id the primary key, which means unique and not NULL. NOT NULL forbids missing names. UNIQUE forbids two departments with the same name, which makes name an alternate key. building has no constraint, so it may be NULL.

The student table with every kind of constraint: CREATE TABLE student (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL, dept_id CHAR(5) REFERENCES department(dept_id) ON DELETE RESTRICT, cgpa DECIMAL(3,2) CHECK (cgpa BETWEEN 0 AND 4), city VARCHAR(30) DEFAULT 'Dhaka'); REFERENCES makes dept_id a foreign key. ON DELETE RESTRICT means a department cannot be deleted while students point to it. CHECK enforces a rule on every row. DEFAULT gives a value when the insert does not mention the column. Each of these is one of the integrity constraints from lesson 5, now written as code.

Table-level constraints: When a constraint involves more than one column, write it after the columns. CREATE TABLE enroll (student_id INT, course_code CHAR(6), grade VARCHAR(2), PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_code), FOREIGN KEY (student_id) REFERENCES student(id) ON DELETE CASCADE, FOREIGN KEY (course_code) REFERENCES course(code)); The composite primary key says each student-course pair appears once. CASCADE on student_id means that if a student record is deleted, that student's enrollments go too. You can also name constraints, like CONSTRAINT chk_cgpa CHECK (cgpa <= 4), so error messages are easier to read and the constraint can be dropped later by name.

Order of creation: Because student refers to department, department must be created first. Because enroll refers to both student and course, it must come last. If you try to create the tables in the wrong order, many systems complain that the referenced table does not exist. The same logic applies to dropping: drop enroll before student, or the foreign key will block it.

Inserting rows: INSERT INTO department VALUES ('CSE', 'Computer Science and Engineering', 'Building A'); gives values in column order. Safer is to name the columns: INSERT INTO student (id, name, dept_id, cgpa) VALUES (1, 'Rina', 'CSE', 3.80); city was not mentioned, so it gets the default 'Dhaka'. Naming columns protects you if someone later adds or reorders columns. Many systems let you insert several rows at once: INSERT INTO course VALUES ('CSE101', 'Intro to Programming', 3, 'CSE'), ('CSE201', 'Data Structures', 3, 'CSE'); Text values go inside single quotes. Numbers do not.

Watching the constraints work: Try INSERT INTO student VALUES (2, 'Sami', 'CSE', 4.50, 'Chattogram'); The DBMS rejects it: the CHECK constraint failed, because 4.50 is above 4. Try a student with dept_id 'MATH': rejected, the foreign key failed. Try a second student with id 1: rejected, the primary key must be unique. Try a student with name NULL: rejected by NOT NULL. Every one of these was tested on SQLite while writing this lesson, and every big DBMS behaves the same way, with slightly different error messages. This is the reason to put rules in the database: no program can sneak bad data past them.

Auto-numbered keys: Remember surrogate keys from lesson 5. You rarely want to pick each new id by hand, so the DBMS can hand them out. The SQL standard writes it as id INT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY. MySQL uses AUTO_INCREMENT, PostgreSQL also accepts the older SERIAL, and in SQLite a column declared INTEGER PRIMARY KEY gets the next number automatically when you leave it out. Then INSERT INTO payment (student_id, amount) VALUES (1, 2500) gets id 1, the next insert gets id 2, and so on. Two cashiers inserting at the same moment never receive the same number, because the DBMS hands out the numbers safely. Do not expect the numbers to have no gaps, though: a cancelled insert can use up a number and leave a hole, which is perfectly normal.

Inserting from a query: You can fill a table with the result of a SELECT. INSERT INTO dean_list (id, name) SELECT id, name FROM student WHERE cgpa >= 3.75; copies all qualifying students in one statement. This is handy for making archive tables, like copying last year's results into results_2025 before cleaning the main table.

Updating rows: UPDATE student SET cgpa = 3.85, city = 'Gazipur' WHERE id = 1; changes the chosen columns in every row that matches the WHERE condition. Without WHERE, every row is updated. UPDATE student SET cgpa = 3.90; gives every student a CGPA of 3.90, a famous disaster that has happened in real companies. Always write the WHERE clause first, and it is a good habit to run the same condition as a SELECT before running the UPDATE, to see exactly which rows will change. An update can use the old value: UPDATE course SET credits = credits + 1 WHERE code = 'CSE201'.

Deleting rows: DELETE FROM enroll WHERE student_id = 4 AND course_code = 'BBA101'; removes matching rows. Like UPDATE, DELETE without WHERE removes every row, though the table itself stays. Deleting a parent row triggers the foreign key rules: deleting the CSE department is refused because of ON DELETE RESTRICT, while deleting a student deletes the student's enrollments because of ON DELETE CASCADE.

ALTER TABLE: Requirements change, and ALTER changes the structure without losing the data. ALTER TABLE student ADD phone VARCHAR(15); adds a column, with NULL in the existing rows. ALTER TABLE student DROP COLUMN phone; removes it. You can also add or drop constraints, rename columns or change types, though the exact syntax differs between systems, so check the manual of your DBMS. Adding a NOT NULL column to a table with rows usually needs a DEFAULT, otherwise the existing rows would break the rule.

DROP and TRUNCATE: DROP TABLE enroll; deletes the table completely: rows, structure, constraints and indexes, all gone. TRUNCATE TABLE enroll; removes all rows but keeps the empty table. TRUNCATE is usually much faster than DELETE without WHERE on big tables, because it does not remove rows one by one, but it cannot have a WHERE condition and, in several systems, it does not fire row triggers. SQLite has no TRUNCATE; there you write DELETE FROM enroll. Treat DROP with great respect: in production, many companies allow it only to the DBA.

Transactions in one paragraph: A sequence of changes can be grouped. BEGIN; UPDATE account SET balance = balance - 500 WHERE no = 'A'; UPDATE account SET balance = balance + 500 WHERE no = 'B'; COMMIT; COMMIT makes the changes permanent. ROLLBACK instead of COMMIT undoes everything since BEGIN, as if nothing happened. Many tools run each statement in its own transaction automatically, called autocommit. Lessons 20 to 23 explain how the DBMS keeps these promises.

Real-life example 1, setting up a coaching centre app: A developer in Mirpur builds an app for a coaching centre. First, CREATE TABLE batch, then student with a foreign key to batch, then payment with a foreign key to student and CHECK (amount > 0). The receptionist's app runs INSERT for each new admission and payment. At the end of the year, the developer runs INSERT INTO payment_2025 SELECT * FROM payment WHERE year = 2025 and then deletes those rows from payment. When the owner asks for a 'guardian phone' field, ALTER TABLE student ADD guardian_phone does it without touching old data.

Real-life example 2, a Daraz price update: During a sale, prices of all items in the 'Mobile' category drop by ten percent. One statement does it: UPDATE product SET price = price * 0.9 WHERE category = 'Mobile'; Before running it, the engineer runs SELECT COUNT(*) FROM product WHERE category = 'Mobile' to check the number of affected rows, and wraps the update in a transaction, so that if the count after the update looks wrong, ROLLBACK brings everything back.

Common mistakes and exam favourites: Forgetting WHERE in UPDATE or DELETE. Using double quotes for text values; in standard SQL, text uses single quotes and double quotes are for names of columns or tables. Storing money in FLOAT. Creating child tables before parents. Confusing DELETE (rows, can use WHERE), TRUNCATE (all rows, keeps table) and DROP (whole table). Thinking CHAR and VARCHAR are the same. Exams usually ask you to write CREATE TABLE statements with all keys and constraints for a given schema, and to explain the difference between DELETE, TRUNCATE and DROP.

Recap: SQL is the standard relational language, born at IBM in the 1970s. DDL defines structure with CREATE, ALTER and DROP; DML changes data with INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE; DCL and TCL handle permissions and transactions. Column types and constraints, PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK and DEFAULT, turn the integrity rules of the relational model into code that the DBMS enforces on every change. Next lesson, you will start asking questions with SELECT.
key_points: SQL started as SEQUEL at IBM in the 1970s and became an ANSI standard in 1986; products follow it with small dialect differences.
DDL (CREATE, ALTER, DROP) defines structure; DML (SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) works with rows; DCL (GRANT, REVOKE) handles permissions; TCL (COMMIT, ROLLBACK) handles transactions.
Use DECIMAL for money, VARCHAR for variable text, CHAR for fixed-length codes, DATE/TIMESTAMP for time.
Constraints PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY ... REFERENCES, NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK and DEFAULT make the DBMS enforce the rules on every change.
UPDATE and DELETE without WHERE affect every row; test the condition with SELECT first.
DELETE removes chosen rows, TRUNCATE removes all rows but keeps the table, DROP removes the whole table.
Create parent tables before child tables, and drop child tables before parents.
lessons.tip: Install a free tool like DB Browser for SQLite, or use any online SQL playground, and type every statement from this lesson yourself. Then deliberately break each constraint and read the error message. Seeing the database refuse bad data teaches more than any definition.
lessons.task: Write CREATE TABLE statements for a small mobile recharge shop: customer(phone, name), operator(code, name) and recharge(id, phone, operator_code, amount, recharge_time). Add primary keys, foreign keys, NOT NULL where needed and CHECK (amount BETWEEN 10 AND 5000). Then write three INSERTs that work and three that each break a different constraint.

quiz.q: Which statement removes all rows from a table but keeps the table structure, and cannot use a WHERE condition?
quiz.explain: TRUNCATE empties the table but keeps its structure; DROP removes the table itself, and DELETE can use WHERE.

quiz.q: A table has CHECK (cgpa BETWEEN 0 AND 4). What happens to INSERT ... VALUES (2, 'Sami', 'CSE', 4.50, 'Chattogram')?
options: The row is inserted with cgpa 4.00
The row is inserted with cgpa NULL
The CHECK is ignored for inserts
quiz.explain: Every new or changed row must satisfy the CHECK condition; 4.50 is outside 0 to 4, so the DBMS rejects it.

quiz.q: What does UPDATE student SET cgpa = 3.90; do?
options: Gives an error because WHERE is required
Updates only students with a NULL CGPA
Sets the CGPA of every student to 3.90
quiz.explain: Without a WHERE clause, UPDATE changes every row of the table.

quiz.q: Which data type is the best choice for storing taka amounts in a bank database?
quiz.explain: DECIMAL stores exact decimal values; FLOAT is approximate and can cause rounding errors with money.

quiz.q: enroll has a foreign key to student with ON DELETE CASCADE. What happens when a student row is deleted?
options: The student's enroll rows are deleted too
The student's enroll rows keep the old id
The student's enroll rows get student_id set to 0
quiz.explain: CASCADE spreads the delete to the child rows that reference the deleted parent.

lessons.title: SQL II: Basic Queries with SELECT
lessons.content:
Imagine a librarian who never gets tired. You walk up and say: 'Give me the names of all CSE students with CGPA above 3, best first.' In less than a blink, she hands you a neat list. That librarian is the SELECT statement. It is the most used statement in all of SQL; developers write far more SELECTs than everything else put together. This lesson teaches the core of it: choosing columns, filtering rows, sorting, patterns, and the tricky world of NULL.

The running data: We keep using student(id, name, dept_id, cgpa, city) with five rows: 1 Rina, CSE, 3.80, Dhaka; 2 Sami, CSE, 3.20, Chattogram; 3 Tuli, EEE, 3.55, Sylhet; 4 Upol, BBA, 2.90, Dhaka; 5 Nadia, CSE, NULL, Khulna. Every result shown in this lesson was checked by running the query in SQLite on exactly these rows.

The basic shape: SELECT columns FROM table WHERE condition; SELECT says which columns you want, FROM says which table, WHERE says which rows. SELECT name, cgpa FROM student WHERE dept_id = 'CSE' AND cgpa > 3.0; returns Rina 3.80 and Sami 3.20. Compare this with relational algebra: WHERE is selection and the SELECT list is projection. So SELECT in SQL is really pi in algebra, a classic naming trap, since algebra's sigma is SQL's WHERE.

SELECT star: SELECT * FROM student; returns every column of every row. It is handy for a quick look, but in real programs it is better to list columns. If someone later adds a large column, like a photo, SELECT * would suddenly pull it everywhere, slowing every screen.

Expressions and aliases: The SELECT list can calculate. SELECT name, cgpa * 25 AS score FROM student WHERE id = 1; returns Rina with score 95.0. AS gives the result column a friendly name, called an alias. You can do arithmetic with plus, minus, times and divide, and use functions like UPPER(name), LENGTH(name) or ROUND(cgpa, 1). Text can be joined with || in standard SQL, as in name || ' from ' || city, though MySQL uses CONCAT instead. Tables can have aliases too: FROM student s, then write s.name. This becomes essential in joins.

DISTINCT: SQL keeps duplicate rows unless you ask it not to. SELECT city FROM student; returns five rows, with Dhaka twice. SELECT DISTINCT city FROM student; returns four: Chattogram, Dhaka, Khulna and Sylhet. DISTINCT applies to the whole row of selected columns, so SELECT DISTINCT dept_id, city treats each pair as one item. Removing duplicates costs work, so the DBMS only does it when you ask.

Comparison operators: = equal, <> not equal (many systems also accept !=), <, >, <= and >=. Strings are compared in alphabetical order, so name < 'N' gives names starting with A to M. Combine conditions with AND, OR and NOT, and use brackets to be clear. AND binds tighter than OR, so dept_id = 'CSE' OR dept_id = 'EEE' AND cgpa > 3.5 means CSE students, plus EEE students above 3.5, which is probably not what you meant. Brackets fix it: (dept_id = 'CSE' OR dept_id = 'EEE') AND cgpa > 3.5.

BETWEEN: cgpa BETWEEN 3.0 AND 3.6 means cgpa >= 3.0 AND cgpa <= 3.6. Both ends are included. On our data it returns Sami (3.20) and Tuli (3.55). NOT BETWEEN gives the opposite, but, as you will see shortly, still not Nadia, whose CGPA is unknown.

IN: city IN ('Dhaka', 'Sylhet') is a short way to write city = 'Dhaka' OR city = 'Sylhet'. It returns Rina, Tuli and Upol. IN gets more powerful in lesson 11, where the list can come from another query.

LIKE patterns: LIKE matches text against a pattern. The percent sign % matches any sequence of characters, even none. The underscore _ matches exactly one character. name LIKE 'R%' finds names starting with R. name LIKE '%a' finds names ending with a, giving Rina and Nadia. name LIKE '_a%' finds names whose second letter is a, giving Sami and Nadia. title LIKE '%Data%' finds Data Structures. Whether LIKE is case-sensitive depends on the system and its settings: SQLite ignores case for English letters by default, PostgreSQL does not.

ORDER BY: Rows in a table have no guaranteed order, so if order matters you must ask for it. ORDER BY cgpa DESC sorts from highest to lowest; ASC, the default, sorts lowest first. You can sort by several columns: ORDER BY dept_id, cgpa DESC sorts by department, and inside each department by CGPA from highest. Where NULL values go when sorting differs between systems: some put them first, others last, and many support NULLS FIRST or NULLS LAST to say so explicitly.

LIMIT and top N: To get only the top few rows, most systems use LIMIT: SELECT name, cgpa FROM student ORDER BY cgpa DESC LIMIT 2; returns Rina and Tuli. The SQL standard writes FETCH FIRST 2 ROWS ONLY, SQL Server uses TOP 2, and OFFSET skips rows, which is how websites show page 2, 3 and so on. LIMIT without ORDER BY gives you any two rows, not the best two, which is a common bug.

NULL, the unknown: NULL means a value is missing or unknown. Nadia's CGPA is NULL, not zero. The rule is simple and strict: any comparison with NULL gives neither true nor false, but a third value, UNKNOWN. Is NULL > 3.5? Unknown. Is NULL = NULL? Also unknown, because two unknown things might or might not be equal. WHERE only keeps rows where the condition is TRUE, so rows with UNKNOWN are dropped.

Three-valued logic: SQL logic has TRUE, FALSE and UNKNOWN. NOT UNKNOWN is UNKNOWN. TRUE AND UNKNOWN is UNKNOWN, but FALSE AND UNKNOWN is FALSE, because AND needs both. TRUE OR UNKNOWN is TRUE, because OR needs only one, while FALSE OR UNKNOWN is UNKNOWN. A surprising result follows: SELECT name FROM student WHERE cgpa < 3.5 OR cgpa >= 3.5; looks like it should return everyone, but it returns only four names. Nadia is missing, because for her both parts are UNKNOWN.

IS NULL: Because cgpa = NULL is never true, SELECT name FROM student WHERE cgpa = NULL; returns nothing at all, even though Nadia's CGPA is NULL. We tested it: zero rows. The correct test is cgpa IS NULL, which returns Nadia, and cgpa IS NOT NULL, which returns the other four. Functions like COALESCE(cgpa, 0) replace NULL with a value for display, but think carefully before treating unknown as zero.

NULL in calculations: NULL also spreads through arithmetic and text. Nadia's cgpa * 25 is NULL, not 0, because an unknown number times 25 is still unknown. In standard SQL, 'CGPA: ' || cgpa is NULL for her too, so the whole label vanishes. Any calculation with a NULL input gives NULL. That is why reports often wrap columns in COALESCE: COALESCE(cgpa, 'not yet') shows the words 'not yet' instead of an empty cell. Also notice the NOT BETWEEN trap promised earlier: WHERE cgpa NOT BETWEEN 3.0 AND 3.6 returns Rina and Upol, and still not Nadia, because NOT UNKNOWN is UNKNOWN.

How a SELECT is evaluated: You write SELECT first, but the DBMS logically works in a different order: FROM picks the tables, WHERE filters rows, then GROUP BY and HAVING, which come in lesson 9, then SELECT computes the output columns, then DISTINCT removes duplicates, then ORDER BY sorts, and finally LIMIT cuts. This explains a common error: you usually cannot use a SELECT alias inside WHERE, because WHERE runs before the alias exists. Many systems do allow the alias in ORDER BY, since ORDER BY runs after SELECT.

Building a query step by step: Question: names and CGPAs of students from Dhaka or Sylhet whose CGPA is known, best first. Step 1, which table? FROM student. Step 2, which rows? WHERE city IN ('Dhaka', 'Sylhet') AND cgpa IS NOT NULL. Step 3, which columns? SELECT name, cgpa. Step 4, which order? ORDER BY cgpa DESC. Put together: SELECT name, cgpa FROM student WHERE city IN ('Dhaka', 'Sylhet') AND cgpa IS NOT NULL ORDER BY cgpa DESC; The result is Rina 3.80, Tuli 3.55, Upol 2.90. Writing FROM and WHERE first, and SELECT last, follows the order in which the DBMS thinks, and it makes long queries much easier to get right.

Comments and readable queries: Two dashes start a comment that runs to the end of the line, like -- top students for the dean, and /* ... */ wraps a longer comment. Put each clause on its own line, write keywords in capitals and give tables short aliases. SQL does not care about spaces or line breaks, but the next person who reads your query, possibly you after six months, will care a lot.

Names that clash with keywords: Some words, like order, group, user and select, are reserved by SQL. If a table is called order, SELECT * FROM order; confuses the parser. Standard SQL lets you quote such names with double quotes: SELECT * FROM "order"; MySQL uses backticks instead. The simplest fix is to avoid reserved words when naming tables and columns, for example orders instead of order.

Real-life example 1, a Foodpanda-style search: You open a food app in Banani and search 'biryani', with rating 4 or above, sorted by delivery time. That is roughly SELECT name, rating, delivery_minutes FROM restaurant WHERE area = 'Banani' AND menu_text LIKE '%biryani%' AND rating >= 4 ORDER BY delivery_minutes LIMIT 20; The app then shows page 2 using OFFSET 20. Real apps use search indexes for the text part, but the logic is the same.

Real-life example 2, a school's absent list: A school database has attendance(roll, class, date, status). The headmaster's morning report asks: SELECT roll FROM attendance WHERE class = 8 AND date = '2026-03-10' AND status = 'absent' ORDER BY roll; If the attendance app saved some rows with status NULL because a teacher forgot to mark them, those students do not appear in the absent list or the present list. A careful developer also runs a query WHERE status IS NULL to catch unmarked students. That is three-valued logic in daily life.

Common mistakes and exam favourites: Writing = NULL instead of IS NULL. Forgetting brackets when mixing AND with OR. Expecting a fixed row order without ORDER BY. Thinking SQL removes duplicates like algebra does, without DISTINCT. Using double quotes for string values. Using a SELECT alias inside WHERE. Expecting NOT IN or NOT BETWEEN to include rows with NULL. Typical exams give a table and ask you to write queries with WHERE, LIKE, BETWEEN, IN and ORDER BY, or show a query and ask for its exact output, often including a NULL trap.

Recap: SELECT picks columns, FROM picks tables, WHERE filters rows, ORDER BY sorts and LIMIT cuts. Use DISTINCT to remove duplicates, aliases to rename, expressions to compute, BETWEEN, IN and LIKE as handy filters. NULL means unknown, comparisons with it give UNKNOWN, WHERE keeps only TRUE rows, and IS NULL is the right test. The logical order of evaluation is FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, DISTINCT, ORDER BY, LIMIT. Next lesson adds counting, averages and grouping.
key_points: SELECT columns FROM table WHERE condition: the SELECT list is projection and WHERE is selection.
SQL keeps duplicates unless you write DISTINCT, unlike pure relational algebra.
BETWEEN includes both ends; IN tests membership in a list; LIKE uses % for any characters and _ for exactly one.
Without ORDER BY, row order is not guaranteed; LIMIT without ORDER BY gives arbitrary rows.
Any comparison with NULL is UNKNOWN; WHERE keeps only TRUE rows; use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL.
In three-valued logic, TRUE OR UNKNOWN is TRUE and FALSE AND UNKNOWN is FALSE; other mixes with UNKNOWN stay UNKNOWN.
Logical order: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, DISTINCT, ORDER BY, LIMIT.
lessons.tip: Before running any query, predict its output by hand on a small table, then run it and compare. When your prediction is wrong, it is almost always because of NULL, missing brackets around OR, or duplicate rows. Those three traps cover most beginner bugs.
lessons.task: Make a five-row table of your friends with name, district, age and phone, leaving one person's age as NULL. Write queries for: friends older than 20, friends whose name starts with 'S', friends from two chosen districts using IN, and everyone sorted by age. Predict each answer first and notice what happens to the NULL row.

quiz.q: What does SELECT name FROM student WHERE cgpa = NULL; return when Nadia's CGPA is NULL?
quiz.explain: cgpa = NULL is UNKNOWN for every row, and WHERE keeps only TRUE rows, so nothing is returned. Use IS NULL instead.

quiz.q: Which pattern finds names whose second letter is 'a'?
quiz.explain: The underscore matches exactly one character, then 'a', then % matches anything after it.

quiz.q: In SQL's three-valued logic, what is FALSE AND UNKNOWN?
quiz.explain: AND needs both sides to be true; since one side is already FALSE, the result is FALSE whatever the unknown side is.

quiz.q: cgpa BETWEEN 3.0 AND 3.6 is the same as:
quiz.explain: BETWEEN includes both boundary values.

quiz.q: Why can you usually not use a SELECT alias inside the WHERE clause?
options: Aliases can only be used for tables
Aliases are deleted after ORDER BY
WHERE is evaluated before the SELECT list creates the alias
quiz.explain: Logically, FROM and WHERE run before SELECT, so the alias does not exist yet when WHERE is evaluated.

lessons.title: SQL III: Aggregates, GROUP BY and HAVING
lessons.content:
At the end of every month, a shopkeeper in Kawran Bazar does not want to see every single sale. He wants summaries: how much did I sell in total, which product sold most, which day was busiest. Bosses, teachers and governments all think in summaries: average marks, number of patients, total revenue per district. SQL's aggregate functions and the GROUP BY clause turn thousands of rows into a few meaningful numbers. This lesson shows how they work, how NULL affects them, and the classic difference between WHERE and HAVING.

The running data: student has five rows: Rina (CSE, 3.80, Dhaka), Sami (CSE, 3.20, Chattogram), Tuli (EEE, 3.55, Sylhet), Upol (BBA, 2.90, Dhaka) and Nadia (CSE, NULL, Khulna). enroll has six rows: CSE101 taken by Rina (A), Sami (B+) and Tuli (B); CSE201 by Rina (A-); EEE101 by Tuli (A); BBA101 by Upol (B). Every result below was checked in SQLite on exactly this data.

The five aggregate functions: COUNT counts, SUM adds, AVG averages, MIN finds the smallest and MAX the largest. They take many values and return one. SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(cgpa), AVG(cgpa), MIN(cgpa), MAX(cgpa), SUM(cgpa) FROM student; returns 5, 4, 3.3625, 2.90, 3.80 and 13.45. Look closely: two different counts, and an average that is not 13.45 divided by 5.

COUNT(*) versus COUNT(column): COUNT(*) counts rows, all of them, whatever they contain: 5. COUNT(cgpa) counts only the non-NULL values in that column: 4, because Nadia's CGPA is NULL. COUNT(DISTINCT city) counts different non-NULL values: 4 cities, because Dhaka appears twice. Choosing the wrong COUNT is one of the most common reporting bugs: 'how many students?' needs COUNT(*), while 'how many students have a CGPA yet?' needs COUNT(cgpa).

NULLs and aggregates: Every aggregate except COUNT(*) simply ignores NULL values. SUM(cgpa) is 3.80 + 3.20 + 3.55 + 2.90 = 13.45, without Nadia. AVG(cgpa) is that sum divided by the count of non-NULL values: 13.45 / 4 = 3.3625. If you treated Nadia's NULL as zero, with AVG(COALESCE(cgpa, 0)), you would get 13.45 / 5 = 2.69, a very different and probably unfair number. Decide on purpose which one your report means.

Aggregates over nothing: What if no row matches? SELECT COUNT(*) FROM student WHERE dept_id = 'MATH'; returns 0. But SELECT SUM(cgpa) FROM student WHERE dept_id = 'MATH'; returns NULL, not 0, because there were no values to add. AVG, MIN and MAX of an empty set are also NULL. Programs that print totals often wrap them as COALESCE(SUM(amount), 0) so the screen shows 0 taka instead of a blank.

GROUP BY, one row per group: Without GROUP BY, an aggregate squeezes the whole table into one row. GROUP BY splits the rows into groups that share the same value, then computes the aggregate for each group separately. SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*) AS n, AVG(cgpa) FROM student GROUP BY dept_id; returns BBA 1 2.90, CSE 3 3.50, EEE 1 3.55. In the CSE group there are three students, but the average is (3.80 + 3.20) / 2 = 3.50, because Nadia's NULL is skipped while she is still counted by COUNT(*).

Picture it as sorting into baskets: Imagine writing each student's details on a card and dropping the cards into baskets labelled by department. Then, for each basket, you count the cards and average the CGPAs. Each basket becomes one row of the answer. Grouping by city instead gives four baskets: Chattogram 1, Dhaka 2, Khulna 1, Sylhet 1.

The golden rule of GROUP BY: In a grouped query, every column in the SELECT list must either be in the GROUP BY clause or be inside an aggregate function. SELECT dept_id, name, COUNT(*) FROM student GROUP BY dept_id; is wrong, because the CSE basket has three names, so which name should the single CSE row show? Standard SQL and PostgreSQL reject this query. MySQL, depending on its settings, and SQLite accept it and pick a value from some row, which gives misleading results. Follow the rule and your queries will work everywhere.

Grouping by several columns: GROUP BY dept_id, city makes a group for every distinct department-city pair. With our data, CSE-Dhaka, CSE-Chattogram, CSE-Khulna, EEE-Sylhet and BBA-Dhaka each get one row. More columns in GROUP BY means smaller, more detailed groups.

HAVING, filtering groups: WHERE filters rows before grouping. HAVING filters groups after grouping, and it can use aggregates. 'Departments with at least two students' is SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*) FROM student GROUP BY dept_id HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2; which returns only CSE 3. You cannot write WHERE COUNT(*) >= 2, because when WHERE runs, the groups do not exist yet and nothing has been counted.

WHERE and HAVING together: SELECT dept_id, AVG(cgpa) FROM student WHERE city <> 'Khulna' GROUP BY dept_id HAVING AVG(cgpa) > 3.0; First WHERE removes Nadia, the Khulna row. Then the remaining rows are grouped: BBA with Upol, CSE with Rina and Sami, EEE with Tuli. Then HAVING keeps groups whose average is above 3.0: CSE at 3.50 and EEE at 3.55. BBA at 2.90 is dropped. A good habit: if a condition is about single rows, put it in WHERE, because filtering early means less work for grouping; if it is about a group's total, put it in HAVING.

The full evaluation order again: FROM, then WHERE, then GROUP BY, then HAVING, then SELECT, then DISTINCT, then ORDER BY, then LIMIT. You can ORDER BY an aggregate: SELECT course_code, COUNT(*) FROM enroll GROUP BY course_code ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC; puts CSE101, with three students, first. The other three courses each have one student, and because they tie, their order among themselves is not guaranteed unless you add a second sort column.

CASE expressions: CASE is SQL's if-else, and it works inside any expression. SELECT name, CASE WHEN cgpa >= 3.5 THEN 'Excellent' WHEN cgpa >= 3.0 THEN 'Good' WHEN cgpa IS NULL THEN 'New' ELSE 'Needs help' END AS remark FROM student; gives Rina and Tuli Excellent, Sami Good, Upol Needs help and Nadia New. The WHEN conditions are checked from top to bottom and the first true one wins, so order matters: if the 3.0 test came first, Rina would be labelled Good.

Conditional counting with CASE: Combine CASE with SUM to count several things in one pass. SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN grade LIKE 'A%' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS a_grades FROM enroll; returns 3: Rina's A and A-, and Tuli's A. You could add more columns in the same query for B grades, F grades and so on. This trick builds whole report tables, like a result sheet with counts of each grade per course, using one scan of the data.

A worked report: The exam controller wants, for each course, the number of students and the number of A-range grades, showing only courses with at least one student, most popular first. SELECT course_code, COUNT(*) AS students, SUM(CASE WHEN grade LIKE 'A%' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS a_count FROM enroll GROUP BY course_code HAVING COUNT(*) >= 1 ORDER BY students DESC; CSE101 comes first with 3 students and 1 A-range grade. Joining with course to show titles is the topic of the next lesson.

Counting per student, and who goes missing: SELECT student_id, COUNT(*) AS courses FROM enroll GROUP BY student_id; returns Rina 2, Sami 1, Tuli 2 and Upol 1. Nadia is not in the answer at all, not even with 0, because she has no rows in enroll, and GROUP BY can only make groups out of rows that exist. To show Nadia with 0 courses, you must start from the student table and use an outer join, which is exactly what the next lesson teaches. Remember this: a group with zero rows never appears by itself.

Finding the top group: 'Which department has the highest average CGPA?' One simple answer is SELECT dept_id, AVG(cgpa) AS avg_cgpa FROM student GROUP BY dept_id ORDER BY avg_cgpa DESC LIMIT 1; which returns EEE with 3.55. Two warnings. First, with ties, LIMIT 1 silently hides the other winners; lesson 11 shows a subquery that returns all of them. Second, EEE wins here with only one student, so real reports often add HAVING COUNT(cgpa) >= 5 to ignore tiny groups that win by luck.

An average of averages is not the average: The overall average CGPA is 3.3625. The three department averages are 3.50, 3.55 and 2.90, and their simple average is about 3.32. They differ because CSE has two known CGPAs while EEE and BBA have one each, so averaging the averages gives small departments too much weight. When a report needs the true overall figure, compute it from the raw rows, or weight each group by its count. This mistake shows up in real newspapers and company reports, not only in exams.

NULL in the grouping column: If several rows have NULL in the GROUP BY column, for example students whose department is not yet chosen, SQL puts all of them together in one group with a NULL label. This is a little odd, since elsewhere NULL is never equal to NULL, but it is what the standard says, and it is useful: the report shows one row for 'unknown department' with its count, instead of losing those students.

Real-life example 1, bKash monthly summary: A merchant dashboard shows total collection per day this month. SELECT DATE(txn_time) AS day, COUNT(*) AS payments, SUM(amount) AS total FROM payment WHERE merchant_id = 501 AND txn_time >= '2026-03-01' GROUP BY DATE(txn_time) ORDER BY day; WHERE keeps one merchant and one month, GROUP BY makes one row per day, and the aggregates give the number of payments and the taka collected. A HAVING SUM(amount) > 50000 would highlight the busy days only.

Real-life example 2, election results: Each polling centre reports votes as rows of votes(centre_id, constituency, candidate, count). The constituency result is SELECT candidate, SUM(count) AS total FROM votes WHERE constituency = 'Dhaka-10' GROUP BY candidate ORDER BY total DESC; The top row is the winner. If one centre's report is missing and stored with count NULL, SUM silently ignores it, so officials also check COUNT(*) against COUNT(count) to make sure every centre has reported.

Common mistakes and exam favourites: Using WHERE with an aggregate instead of HAVING. Selecting a non-grouped, non-aggregated column. Thinking AVG counts NULL as zero. Using COUNT(column) when you meant COUNT(*). Expecting SUM over no rows to be 0. Putting row conditions in HAVING, which works but wastes effort. Typical exam questions: find the department with the highest average, list courses with more than N students, explain WHERE versus HAVING, and compute the exact output of an aggregate query on a small table that contains NULLs.

Recap: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX turn many values into one; all except COUNT(*) ignore NULL. GROUP BY splits rows into groups and computes aggregates per group. Every selected column must be grouped or aggregated. WHERE filters rows before grouping and HAVING filters groups after. CASE adds if-else logic and, inside SUM, enables conditional counting. Next lesson brings in joins, so you can combine student, course and enroll in one query.
key_points: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX reduce many values to one; all except COUNT(*) ignore NULL.
COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(col) counts non-NULL values; COUNT(DISTINCT col) counts different non-NULL values.
AVG divides by the number of non-NULL values; SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX over no rows return NULL.
GROUP BY makes one result row per group; every selected column must be grouped or aggregated.
WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after grouping and may use aggregates.
CASE WHEN ... THEN ... ELSE ... END is SQL's if-else; the first true condition wins.
SUM(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) counts rows that meet a condition inside a group.
lessons.tip: For every grouped query, say in words: 'one row per ___'. If you cannot fill the blank, you do not yet know your GROUP BY. If any selected column could have two different values inside one group, the query is wrong.
lessons.task: Write down a week of your family's expenses as rows: day, category (food, transport, mobile, other) and amount, with one amount left blank. On paper, compute: total per category, average per day, number of expenses per category, and categories whose total is above 500 taka. Then check which answers change if the blank is treated as 0.

quiz.q: student has 5 rows and Nadia's cgpa is NULL. What are COUNT(*) and COUNT(cgpa)?
quiz.explain: COUNT(*) counts all rows (5); COUNT(cgpa) counts only non-NULL values (4).

quiz.q: CGPAs are 3.80, 3.20 and NULL in the CSE group. What is AVG(cgpa) for CSE?
quiz.explain: AVG ignores NULL, so it is (3.80 + 3.20) / 2 = 3.50.

quiz.q: Which query correctly lists departments with more than 10 students?
options: SELECT dept_id FROM student WHERE COUNT(*) > 10 GROUP BY dept_id
SELECT dept_id FROM student GROUP BY dept_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 10
SELECT dept_id FROM student HAVING id > 10
quiz.explain: Conditions on aggregates belong in HAVING, which runs after GROUP BY; WHERE cannot use COUNT.

quiz.q: What does SELECT SUM(amount) FROM payment WHERE 1 = 0; return?
quiz.explain: No rows match, so there is nothing to add; SUM over an empty set is NULL. Use COALESCE(SUM(amount), 0) to show 0.

quiz.q: Why is SELECT dept_id, name, COUNT(*) FROM student GROUP BY dept_id a bad query?
options: name is neither grouped nor aggregated, so one group may have many names
COUNT(*) cannot be used with GROUP BY
GROUP BY must come before FROM
quiz.explain: Each group produces one row, but a group can contain several different names; standard SQL rejects such a query.

lessons.title: SQL IV: Joins, Putting Tables Back Together
lessons.content:
In lesson 4 we cut the university's data into neat separate tables: students in one, departments in another, courses in a third and enrollments in a fourth. That was the right thing to do, because it removes duplication. But the people using the database do not think in separate tables. The exam office wants one sheet: student name, course title, grade. A join is how SQL glues the pieces back together for the moment of the question, without storing the duplication. If SELECT is the most used statement, joins are the most used feature inside it.

The running data: student has Rina (1, CSE), Sami (2, CSE), Tuli (3, EEE), Upol (4, BBA) and Nadia (5, CSE). department has CSE in Building A, EEE in Building B and BBA in Building C. course has CSE101 Intro to Programming, CSE201 Data Structures, EEE101 Electrical Circuits and BBA101 Principles of Accounting. enroll has six rows: Rina in CSE101 (A) and CSE201 (A-), Sami in CSE101 (B+), Tuli in CSE101 (B) and EEE101 (A), Upol in BBA101 (B). Nadia has taken nothing yet. Every result below was run in SQLite on this data.

Why joins are needed: Ask 'what is the name of Rina's department?' The student table only says dept_id = 'CSE'. The full name, Computer Science and Engineering, lives in department. The answer needs a row from each table, matched on the shared value CSE. That matching, row by row, on a condition, is a join. In relational algebra it is a Cartesian product followed by a selection; in SQL you write it directly.

The old style, comma join: SELECT s.name, d.name FROM student s, department d WHERE s.dept_id = d.dept_id; Listing two tables in FROM makes a Cartesian product, here 5 times 3 = 15 combinations, and WHERE keeps only the matching ones. It works and you will see it in old code and many textbooks. Its danger: forget the WHERE condition and you silently get all 15 combinations, most of them nonsense.

INNER JOIN with ON: The modern style is SELECT s.name, d.name FROM student s JOIN department d ON s.dept_id = d.dept_id; JOIN means INNER JOIN by default. The ON clause holds the join condition, and WHERE is left free for real filters. The result has five rows: Rina, Sami and Nadia with Computer Science and Engineering, Tuli with Electrical and Electronic Engineering, and Upol with Business Administration. Each student has exactly one department, so each appears once.

What inner means: An inner join returns only rows that find a partner. SELECT s.name, e.course_code FROM student s JOIN enroll e ON s.id = e.student_id; returns six rows: Rina twice, Tuli twice, Sami once and Upol once. Nadia is missing, because no enroll row has student_id 5. Notice also that Rina appears twice: a join produces one output row for every matching pair, so a student with two courses gives two rows. Both effects, missing rows and repeated rows, surprise beginners.

Table aliases and qualified names: When two tables both have a column with the same name, like name in student and in department, you must say which one you mean: s.name or d.name. Writing just name gives an 'ambiguous column' error. Short aliases like s, d, e and c keep long queries readable. It is good practice to qualify every column in a join, even when it is not ambiguous, so readers know where each value comes from.

USING and NATURAL JOIN: If the join columns have the same name in both tables, JOIN department USING (dept_id) is a short form, and the output has only one dept_id column. NATURAL JOIN goes further and joins on every column with the same name. That is dangerous here: student and department both have dept_id and name, so student NATURAL JOIN department requires the student's name to equal the department's name. We ran it: zero rows. This is exactly the trap described in lesson 6, and it is why many teams ban NATURAL JOIN in real code.

Joining three tables: The exam sheet needs student, enroll and course. SELECT s.name, c.title, e.grade FROM student s JOIN enroll e ON s.id = e.student_id JOIN course c ON c.code = e.course_code ORDER BY s.name; returns six rows, such as Rina, Intro to Programming, A and Rina, Data Structures, A-. Think of it as a chain: student links to enroll by id, enroll links to course by code. A junction table like enroll sits in the middle of almost every many-to-many query. Joining n tables usually needs n - 1 join conditions.

LEFT OUTER JOIN: To keep students who have no enrollments, use a left join. SELECT s.name, e.course_code, e.grade FROM student s LEFT JOIN enroll e ON s.id = e.student_id; returns seven rows: the six matches plus Nadia with NULL course and NULL grade. LEFT JOIN keeps every row of the left table, the one written first, and fills the right side with NULL when no partner exists. The word OUTER is optional: LEFT JOIN and LEFT OUTER JOIN are the same.

Counting with a left join: Last lesson, counting courses per student lost Nadia. Now: SELECT s.name, COUNT(e.course_code) AS courses FROM student s LEFT JOIN enroll e ON s.id = e.student_id GROUP BY s.id, s.name; returns Rina 2, Sami 1, Tuli 2, Upol 1 and Nadia 0. Note the COUNT(e.course_code), not COUNT(*): Nadia's single row has NULL in course_code, so COUNT of that column gives 0, while COUNT(*) would wrongly give 1. This pairing of LEFT JOIN with COUNT of a right-side column is one of the most useful patterns in SQL.

RIGHT and FULL OUTER JOIN: A RIGHT JOIN keeps every row of the right table instead. A LEFT JOIN B is the same as B RIGHT JOIN A, so most people just write left joins and order the tables accordingly. A FULL OUTER JOIN keeps unmatched rows from both sides, filling NULLs wherever a partner is missing. It is useful for comparing two lists, like this month's and last month's customers, to see who is new and who left. MySQL does not support FULL OUTER JOIN directly; SQLite added RIGHT and FULL joins in version 3.39.

The anti-join pattern: 'Students who have taken no course' can be written as SELECT s.name FROM student s LEFT JOIN enroll e ON s.id = e.student_id WHERE e.student_id IS NULL; The left join gives Nadia a row with NULLs, and the WHERE keeps only such rows. Result: Nadia. The same idea finds courses nobody has taken: course LEFT JOIN enroll, WHERE e.course_code IS NULL. In our data every course has a student, so the answer is empty, but if the department adds CSE301 Database Systems tomorrow, it will appear until someone enrolls.

ON versus WHERE in outer joins: This difference matters a lot. SELECT s.name, e.course_code FROM student s LEFT JOIN enroll e ON s.id = e.student_id AND e.course_code = 'CSE101'; keeps all five students, with CSE101 for Rina, Sami and Tuli and NULL for Upol and Nadia. Move the course condition to WHERE, and the query returns only Rina, Sami and Tuli: the WHERE runs after the join and throws away the NULL rows, turning the left join into an inner join. Rule of thumb: conditions about the right-hand table go in ON if you want to keep unmatched left rows.

Self join: A table can be joined with itself using two aliases. Pairs of students from the same city: SELECT a.name, b.name FROM student a JOIN student b ON a.city = b.city AND a.id < b.id; returns Rina and Upol, both from Dhaka. The condition a.id < b.id stops a student from pairing with herself and stops each pair from appearing twice in both orders. Self joins also read hierarchies, like employee joined with employee on supervisor_id = emp_id to print each worker next to the boss's name.

CROSS JOIN: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM student CROSS JOIN course; returns 20, every student paired with every course. Usually this is a mistake, but sometimes it is exactly what you want: generating every possible combination, like every student-subject pair for an empty mark sheet, or every size-colour pair for a shirt in an online shop.

Non-equi joins: The join condition need not be equality. With a table grade_scale(letter, min_mark, max_mark), the query SELECT r.roll, g.letter FROM result r JOIN grade_scale g ON r.mark BETWEEN g.min_mark AND g.max_mark; converts marks into letter grades: 82 matches the row for A+ if A+ is 80 to 100, as in the grading of many Bangladeshi boards and universities. Joins with BETWEEN, < or > are called theta or non-equi joins.

How the DBMS runs a join: You describe the result and the DBMS chooses the method: checking every pair (nested loop), using an index to find partners quickly, sorting both sides and merging them, or building a hash table on one side. Lesson 18 compares these methods and their costs. For you, the practical lesson now is that joins on indexed key columns, like primary and foreign keys, are fast, and joins on unindexed text columns can be slow on big tables.

Real-life example 1, a Pathao trip receipt: Your receipt shows driver name, vehicle plate, pickup, drop and fare. These come from trip, driver and vehicle tables. SELECT d.name, v.plate_no, t.pickup, t.drop_point, t.fare FROM trip t JOIN driver d ON d.driver_id = t.driver_id JOIN vehicle v ON v.plate_no = t.plate_no WHERE t.trip_id = 88412; Three tables, two join conditions, one row out. If a trip is cancelled before a driver accepts, its driver_id is NULL, and the inner join would hide it, so the trip history screen uses a LEFT JOIN to driver.

Real-life example 2, finding inactive customers: A mobile operator wants customers who have not recharged in the last 90 days, to send them an offer. SELECT c.phone FROM customer c LEFT JOIN recharge r ON r.phone = c.phone AND r.recharge_time >= '2026-01-01' WHERE r.phone IS NULL; The date filter sits in ON, so customers with only old recharges still get a NULL row and are kept. Putting the date in WHERE would lose exactly the customers the company is looking for.

Common mistakes and exam favourites: Forgetting the join condition and getting a Cartesian product. Using an inner join when rows without partners must be shown. Putting a right-table condition in WHERE and silently turning a left join into an inner join. Using COUNT(*) instead of COUNT(right_column) after a left join. Using NATURAL JOIN when tables share extra column names. Ambiguous column names. Exams love: write a query joining three tables, list items with no related rows, explain inner versus left versus full outer join with small tables, and give the output of a join that includes duplicates and NULLs.

Recap: A join matches rows of two tables on a condition. INNER JOIN keeps only matched pairs, and a row appears once per match. LEFT, RIGHT and FULL OUTER JOIN keep unmatched rows with NULLs. USING and NATURAL JOIN are short forms, with NATURAL being risky. Self joins use two aliases, CROSS JOIN gives all combinations, and non-equi joins use conditions like BETWEEN. LEFT JOIN with IS NULL finds missing partners. Next lesson adds subqueries, set operations and views.
key_points: A join combines rows from tables that satisfy a join condition, usually primary key = foreign key.
INNER JOIN returns only matching pairs; rows without partners disappear, and a row repeats once per match.
LEFT JOIN keeps every row of the left table, with NULLs for missing right-side values; RIGHT and FULL OUTER work similarly.
After a LEFT JOIN, count with COUNT(right_column), not COUNT(*), to get 0 for rows without partners.
LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right.key IS NULL is the anti-join pattern for 'has no related rows'.
In an outer join, a right-table condition in WHERE turns it into an inner join; put it in ON to keep unmatched rows.
NATURAL JOIN joins on every same-named column and can silently return wrong or empty results.
lessons.tip: Before writing a join, draw the tables as boxes on paper with lines between the key columns. Then walk the path from the table that holds the rows you must keep to the tables that hold the extra details. The table you must not lose rows from goes on the left of a LEFT JOIN.
lessons.task: Draw three small tables on paper: customer(id, name), orders(order_id, customer_id, total) and product(id, name), with one customer who has no orders. Write and evaluate by hand: an inner join of customers and orders, a left join of the same, a count of orders per customer including zero, and the list of customers with no orders.

quiz.q: student has 5 rows; Nadia has no enroll rows, Rina has 2, Tuli has 2, Sami 1, Upol 1. How many rows does student INNER JOIN enroll ON s.id = e.student_id return?
quiz.explain: Inner join gives one row per matching pair: 2 + 1 + 2 + 1 = 6. Nadia has no match and disappears.

quiz.q: The same tables with LEFT JOIN instead. How many rows?
quiz.explain: The six matches stay, and Nadia is kept once with NULLs on the enroll side, giving 7.

quiz.q: Which query lists students who have taken no course?
options: SELECT name FROM student s JOIN enroll e ON s.id = e.student_id WHERE e.grade IS NULL
SELECT name FROM student CROSS JOIN enroll
SELECT s.name FROM student s LEFT JOIN enroll e ON s.id = e.student_id WHERE e.student_id IS NULL
SELECT s.name FROM student s NATURAL JOIN enroll e
quiz.explain: The left join keeps students without enrollments as rows with NULLs, and the IS NULL filter keeps only those.

quiz.q: Why did student NATURAL JOIN department return no rows?
options: Natural joins never work in SQLite
The tables share both dept_id and name, so the student name had to equal the department name
NATURAL JOIN needs an ON clause
quiz.explain: NATURAL JOIN matches on all same-named columns; requiring student.name = department.name removes every row.

quiz.q: After student LEFT JOIN enroll ... GROUP BY student, which expression gives 0 for a student with no courses?
quiz.explain: The unmatched student has one row with NULL in e.course_code; COUNT of that column is 0, while COUNT(*), COUNT(s.id) and SUM(1) give 1.

lessons.title: SQL V: Subqueries, Set Operations and Views
lessons.content:
Some questions have a question hiding inside them. 'Which students scored above the average?' First you need the average, then you compare everyone with it. A good friend would answer the inner question first and then the outer one. SQL lets you write exactly that: a query inside another query, called a subquery or nested query. Together with set operations like UNION and EXCEPT, and with views that save a query under a name, subqueries let you answer almost any question without writing a single line of normal program code.

The running data: student has Rina (CSE, 3.80, Dhaka), Sami (CSE, 3.20, Chattogram), Tuli (EEE, 3.55, Sylhet), Upol (BBA, 2.90, Dhaka) and Nadia (CSE, NULL, Khulna), ids 1 to 5. enroll has Rina in CSE101 (A) and CSE201 (A-), Sami in CSE101 (B+), Tuli in CSE101 (B) and EEE101 (A), and Upol in BBA101 (B). All results were checked in SQLite, except ALL and ANY, which SQLite does not support; those follow the SQL standard.

Scalar subqueries: A subquery that returns exactly one value, one row and one column, can be used anywhere a single value is allowed. SELECT name, cgpa FROM student WHERE cgpa > (SELECT AVG(cgpa) FROM student); The inner query gives 3.3625, and the outer query returns Rina (3.80) and Tuli (3.55). If a scalar subquery returns more than one row, the query fails with an error in most systems, so make sure it really returns one value, for example by using an aggregate or a key condition.

IN with a subquery: IN can take a list produced by a query. SELECT name FROM student WHERE id IN (SELECT student_id FROM enroll WHERE course_code = 'CSE101'); The inner query gives {1, 2, 3}, so the outer query returns Rina, Sami and Tuli. Many IN subqueries can also be written as joins, but IN has a nice property: a student appears at most once even if she matches several inner rows, while a join would repeat her.

NOT IN and its NULL trap: SELECT name FROM student WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT student_id FROM enroll); returns Nadia, the student with no enrollments. That works because student_id in enroll is never NULL. Now watch what happens when the inner list contains a NULL. SELECT name FROM student WHERE cgpa NOT IN (SELECT cgpa FROM student WHERE dept_id = 'CSE'); The inner list is {3.80, 3.20, NULL}. You might expect Tuli and Upol, whose CGPAs are not in that list. The real answer, tested: no rows at all.

Why NOT IN fails: x NOT IN (a, b, NULL) means x <> a AND x <> b AND x <> NULL. The last part, x <> NULL, is always UNKNOWN, and TRUE AND UNKNOWN is UNKNOWN, so no row can ever pass. One NULL in the inner list kills the whole result. With the EEE list {3.55}, which has no NULL, the same query works and returns Rina, Sami and Upol. The safe habits: add WHERE col IS NOT NULL inside the subquery, or use NOT EXISTS, which does not have this problem.

EXISTS and NOT EXISTS: EXISTS (subquery) is true if the subquery returns at least one row, false if it returns none. It never returns UNKNOWN. SELECT s.name FROM student s WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM enroll e WHERE e.student_id = s.id AND e.grade = 'A'); returns students with at least one A: Rina and Tuli. The SELECT 1 inside does not matter; EXISTS only checks whether any row exists. NOT EXISTS is the safest way to write 'has no matching rows'.

Correlated subqueries: The EXISTS example above is correlated: the inner query mentions s.id from the outer query, so logically it is re-evaluated for each outer row. Another example: students above their own department's average. SELECT s.name, s.cgpa FROM student s WHERE s.cgpa > (SELECT AVG(s2.cgpa) FROM student s2 WHERE s2.dept_id = s.dept_id); For Rina, the inner query computes the CSE average, 3.50, and 3.80 passes. Sami's 3.20 does not. Tuli equals her department's average, 3.55, so she does not pass the strict test, and neither does Upol. The answer is Rina only. Optimizers often rewrite correlated subqueries into joins, so they are not always slow, but on big tables it is worth checking.

ALL and ANY: cgpa > ALL (SELECT cgpa FROM student WHERE dept_id = 'BBA') means greater than every value in the list: above 2.90, giving Rina, Sami and Tuli. cgpa > ANY (subquery), also written SOME, means greater than at least one value. A useful identity: = ANY is the same as IN, and <> ALL is the same as NOT IN, including its NULL trap. One more edge case: x > ALL of an empty list is true, because there is nothing to fail against. Many people prefer writing > (SELECT MAX(...)) instead of > ALL, which is clearer.

Subqueries in FROM: A subquery can act as a temporary table, called a derived table, which must have an alias. SELECT dept_id, n FROM (SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*) AS n FROM student GROUP BY dept_id) t WHERE n > 1; returns CSE 3. This lets you filter on the result of a grouping without HAVING, or group results of a previous grouping, which HAVING alone cannot do.

Subqueries in SELECT: A scalar subquery can also produce a column. SELECT name, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM enroll e WHERE e.student_id = s.id) AS courses FROM student s; returns Rina 2, Sami 1, Tuli 2, Upol 1 and Nadia 0. Unlike the inner join version, Nadia is included with 0, because the count of an empty set is 0. This is another way to solve the counting problem from lesson 9.

WITH, common table expressions: Long nested queries are hard to read. A WITH clause gives a subquery a name at the top: WITH dept_avg AS (SELECT dept_id, AVG(cgpa) AS a FROM student GROUP BY dept_id) SELECT dept_id, a FROM dept_avg WHERE a = (SELECT MAX(a) FROM dept_avg); returns EEE 3.55. Unlike ORDER BY ... LIMIT 1 from lesson 9, this returns every department if there is a tie for the top. CTEs make queries read top to bottom like a story. With WITH RECURSIVE, a CTE can even call itself to walk hierarchies, like all prerequisites of a course or all levels of employees under a manager.

Set operations: UNION, INTERSECT and EXCEPT combine the results of two queries that have the same number of columns with compatible types. SELECT city FROM student WHERE dept_id = 'CSE' UNION SELECT city FROM student WHERE dept_id = 'BBA'; returns Chattogram, Dhaka and Khulna: CSE cities plus BBA cities, with Dhaka once. INTERSECT returns rows in both results, EXCEPT returns rows in the first but not the second. Oracle traditionally calls EXCEPT by the name MINUS.

UNION versus UNION ALL: UNION removes duplicates, like the algebra. UNION ALL keeps every row: the same query with UNION ALL returns Dhaka, Chattogram, Khulna and Dhaka again, four rows. Removing duplicates needs sorting or hashing, so UNION ALL is faster. Use UNION ALL whenever you know there are no duplicates, or when you want to keep them, for example when counting things afterwards.

Worked set examples: Students in CSE101 who also took CSE201: SELECT student_id FROM enroll WHERE course_code = 'CSE101' INTERSECT SELECT student_id FROM enroll WHERE course_code = 'CSE201'; gives 1, Rina. Students in CSE101 but not CSE201: replace INTERSECT with EXCEPT, giving 2 and 3, Sami and Tuli. These are exactly the intersection and difference of relational algebra, and they give the same answers as the IN and NOT IN versions, without the NULL trap.

Views: A view is a saved query with a name, which can be used like a table. CREATE VIEW cse_students AS SELECT id, name, cgpa FROM student WHERE dept_id = 'CSE'; Then SELECT * FROM cse_students WHERE cgpa > 3.5; returns Rina. A normal view stores no data, only its definition. Each time you query it, the DBMS merges the view's query with yours and runs the result on the base tables, so a view always shows current data.

Why views help: Views simplify: a complex join can be hidden behind a simple name like result_sheet. Views secure: the accounts office can be given access to a view that shows names and fees but not marks, without access to the base tables. Views give logical data independence: if the base tables are reorganised, the view can be redefined so that old programs keep working, exactly as lesson 2 promised.

Updating through views: Can you INSERT or UPDATE through a view? For simple views, yes: a view over one table, without aggregates, DISTINCT, GROUP BY or joins, where each view row matches exactly one base row, is usually updatable. UPDATE cse_students SET cgpa = 3.90 WHERE id = 1 changes the student table. A view with AVG or GROUP BY is not updatable, because one view row comes from many base rows. Adding WITH CHECK OPTION to a view stops updates that would move a row out of the view, like changing a CSE student's department to EEE through cse_students. Exact rules vary by system; SQLite views, for example, are read-only unless you add special triggers.

Materialized views: Some systems, such as PostgreSQL and Oracle, also offer materialized views, which store the result of the query like a real table. Reading them is fast, but they must be refreshed when the base data changes. They are popular for heavy reports, like a daily sales summary that thousands of managers open every morning.

Real-life example 1, a scholarship board: The university wants students whose CGPA is above their department's average and who have no F grade. WITH dept_avg AS (SELECT dept_id, AVG(cgpa) AS a FROM student GROUP BY dept_id) SELECT s.name FROM student s JOIN dept_avg d ON s.dept_id = d.dept_id WHERE s.cgpa > d.a AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM enroll e WHERE e.student_id = s.id AND e.grade = 'F'); A CTE, a join and a NOT EXISTS work together, and the query reads almost like the rule in the scholarship notice.

Real-life example 2, a Daraz seller portal: Each seller should see only their own orders. The company creates a view seller_orders that joins orders, order_item and product, and the application always adds WHERE seller_id = the logged-in seller. Combined with permissions that let sellers read only the view, this keeps one seller from seeing another's sales. When the company later splits order_item into two tables for speed, only the view's definition changes, and the seller portal keeps working.

Common mistakes and exam favourites: Using NOT IN with a subquery that can return NULL. Writing a scalar subquery that returns several rows. Forgetting the alias of a derived table. Using UNION when UNION ALL is meant, or the other way round. Thinking a view stores a copy of the data. Expecting every view to be updatable. Typical exam tasks: find students above average, find the department with the highest average using a subquery, rewrite an IN query as EXISTS or a join, explain correlated subqueries, and explain views with their advantages.

Recap: Subqueries put a query inside another, as a single value, a list for IN, a test for EXISTS, a derived table in FROM or a column in SELECT. Correlated subqueries refer to the outer row. NOT IN breaks when the list has NULL; NOT EXISTS is safe. ALL and ANY compare against every or some value. WITH names subqueries for readability. UNION, INTERSECT and EXCEPT combine results, with UNION ALL keeping duplicates. Views are named saved queries that simplify, secure and protect programs from change. Next lesson turns SQL into a programming tool with indexes, triggers and procedures.
key_points: A scalar subquery returns exactly one value and can be used wherever a single value is allowed.
IN tests membership in a subquery's result; EXISTS is true if the subquery returns any row.
NOT IN returns no rows if the subquery's list contains a NULL; NOT EXISTS avoids this trap.
A correlated subquery refers to columns of the outer query and is logically evaluated once per outer row.
WITH (common table expressions) names subqueries; WITH RECURSIVE can walk hierarchies.
UNION, INTERSECT and EXCEPT need compatible columns; UNION removes duplicates, UNION ALL keeps them.
A view is a named stored query, usually holding no data; simple single-table views are updatable, aggregated views are not.
lessons.tip: When a question has the word 'than' or 'every' or 'no' in it, such as 'more than the average', 'took every course' or 'has no orders', think subquery first. Write the inner question as its own query, test it alone, and only then wrap the outer query around it.
lessons.task: Using the five students and six enroll rows of this lesson, write and evaluate by hand: (a) students below the overall average CGPA, (b) students who took at least one course with grade B or B+, using EXISTS, (c) the cities of CSE students EXCEPT the cities of BBA students, and (d) a view called top_students for CGPA at least 3.5. Then check what NOT IN would do if one enroll row had a NULL student_id.

quiz.q: The subquery SELECT cgpa FROM student WHERE dept_id = 'CSE' returns {3.80, 3.20, NULL}. What does WHERE cgpa NOT IN (that subquery) return?
quiz.explain: NOT IN expands to a chain of <> tests joined by AND; the test against NULL is UNKNOWN, so no row can be TRUE.

quiz.q: What does EXISTS (subquery) return when the subquery produces no rows?
quiz.explain: EXISTS is TRUE if at least one row is returned and FALSE otherwise; it never returns UNKNOWN.

quiz.q: What is the difference between UNION and UNION ALL?
options: UNION ALL removes duplicates; UNION keeps them
UNION ALL needs a WHERE clause
UNION removes duplicate rows; UNION ALL keeps them and is usually faster
quiz.explain: UNION removes duplicates, which takes extra work; UNION ALL simply appends all rows.

quiz.q: A subquery that refers to a column of the outer query, like WHERE s2.dept_id = s.dept_id, is called:
quiz.explain: It depends on the current outer row, so logically it is evaluated again for each outer row.

quiz.q: Which statement about a normal (non-materialized) view is true?
options: It stores a copy of the data at creation time
It stores only its query and always shows current base-table data
It cannot be used in a SELECT
quiz.explain: A normal view stores its definition; querying it runs that definition on the base tables, so the data is always current.

lessons.title: SQL VI: Indexes, Triggers, Procedures, Permissions and SQL in Programs
lessons.content:
So far you have used SQL like a very smart calculator: ask a question, get an answer. But a real database also needs speed for millions of rows, automatic reactions when data changes, reusable blocks of logic, rules about who may do what, and a safe way for apps written in Python, Java or Dart to talk to it. This lesson covers those tools: indexes, triggers, stored procedures and functions, cursors, GRANT and REVOKE, and calling SQL from programs. Think of it as moving from asking the database questions to making the database part of your software.

Indexes from the SQL side: An index is an extra structure that helps the DBMS find rows quickly, like the index at the back of a textbook that tells you which page talks about 'normalization'. CREATE INDEX idx_student_city ON student(city); builds an index on the city column. After that, SELECT name FROM student WHERE city = 'Dhaka' can jump straight to the Dhaka entries instead of reading every row. We checked with SQLite's EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN, and it reported SEARCH student USING INDEX idx_student_city, instead of a full scan. The query text stays the same; only its speed changes, which is physical data independence in action.

What indexes cost: Indexes are not free. Each index takes disk space, and every INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE must also update every index on that table. A table with ten indexes makes writes slower. So you index columns that are searched or joined often, like foreign keys, and columns used in WHERE and ORDER BY, and skip columns that are rarely queried. Most systems automatically create an index for every PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE constraint. CREATE UNIQUE INDEX also enforces uniqueness, and DROP INDEX removes an index. Lesson 17 explains how indexes work inside, using B+ trees and hashing.

Composite indexes: An index can cover several columns: CREATE INDEX idx_enroll_course_grade ON enroll(course_code, grade); It is sorted by course_code first, then by grade inside each course, like a phone book sorted by surname, then first name. It helps queries that filter on course_code alone, or on course_code and grade together. It usually does not help a query that filters only on grade, just as a phone book sorted by surname does not help you find everyone named Rahim.

Triggers, the idea: A trigger is a piece of SQL that the DBMS runs automatically when a certain event happens on a table: an INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE. It follows the event-condition-action pattern: when this happens, if this is true, do that. Triggers are like an automatic CCTV system that writes a note in the register every time a door opens. Nobody has to remember to write the note; it just happens.

A trigger example, an audit log: Universities must record every grade change. CREATE TRIGGER trg_grade_change AFTER UPDATE OF grade ON enroll FOR EACH ROW WHEN OLD.grade <> NEW.grade BEGIN INSERT INTO grade_log VALUES (OLD.student_id, OLD.course_code, OLD.grade, NEW.grade, datetime('now')); END; OLD means the row before the change and NEW means the row after. We tested it: after UPDATE enroll SET grade = 'A' WHERE student_id = 2 AND course_code = 'CSE101', grade_log contained student 2, CSE101, B+ to A, with the time. Even if a teacher changes the grade from a different app, the log entry is still written.

BEFORE, AFTER and row versus statement: A BEFORE trigger runs before the change is applied, so it can check or modify the new values, or reject the change. An AFTER trigger runs after the change, which suits logging and updating other tables. FOR EACH ROW triggers run once per affected row; statement-level triggers, supported by systems like PostgreSQL and Oracle, run once per statement no matter how many rows changed. A trigger can stop the operation with an error; in SQLite this is RAISE(ABORT, 'message'), and other systems use their own syntax, such as SIGNAL in MySQL.

Constraints versus triggers: If a rule can be written as a constraint, like NOT NULL, CHECK, UNIQUE or FOREIGN KEY, use the constraint. Constraints are declarative, simple and checked very efficiently. Use triggers for things constraints cannot express: keeping an audit log, updating a running total in another table, or rules that depend on other tables, such as 'a student may not enroll in more than 21 credits per semester'. Too many triggers make a database hard to understand, because changes cause hidden side effects that nobody sees in the application code.

Stored procedures: A stored procedure is a named program saved inside the database, which can take parameters, run several SQL statements, use variables, IF and loops, and be called with one command. In MySQL style: CREATE PROCEDURE enroll_student(IN p_id INT, IN p_code CHAR(6)) BEGIN INSERT INTO enroll (student_id, course_code) VALUES (p_id, p_code); UPDATE course_stats SET seats_taken = seats_taken + 1 WHERE code = p_code; END; then CALL enroll_student(5, 'CSE101'); Each big DBMS has its own procedural language: PL/SQL in Oracle, PL/pgSQL in PostgreSQL, T-SQL in SQL Server, and MySQL's stored routine language. SQLite has no stored procedures at all.

Why use procedures: They keep business logic in one place, so the web app, the mobile app and the admin tool all enrol students the same way. They reduce network trips, since one CALL replaces many separate statements sent from the app. They help security: users can be allowed to run enroll_student without being allowed to touch the enroll table directly. The downside is that the logic is tied to one DBMS's language, which makes changing database products harder, and that some teams find it harder to test and version than normal application code.

Stored functions: A function is like a procedure but returns a value and can be used inside queries. For example, a function grade_point(letter) could return 4.00 for 'A+' and 3.75 for 'A', following the grading scale, and then SELECT student_id, AVG(grade_point(grade)) FROM enroll GROUP BY student_id; computes simple averages. Built-in functions like UPPER, ROUND and COALESCE work the same way; user-defined functions extend the list.

Cursors: SQL works on whole sets of rows at once, but procedural code sometimes needs to handle rows one by one, like sending a personalised SMS to each student. A cursor is a pointer that walks through a query's result row by row: DECLARE a cursor for a SELECT, OPEN it, FETCH each row into variables inside a loop, and CLOSE it at the end. Cursors are slower than set-based SQL, so the rule is: if one UPDATE or INSERT ... SELECT can do the job, prefer it, and use cursors only when each row truly needs separate processing.

Permissions with GRANT and REVOKE: The DBA controls who can do what. GRANT SELECT ON student TO exam_office; lets the exam office read the student table. GRANT SELECT, UPDATE (grade) ON enroll TO teacher_role; lets teachers read enrollments and change only the grade column. REVOKE UPDATE ON enroll FROM teacher_role; takes that right away. Privileges include SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, REFERENCES and EXECUTE for procedures. Roles group privileges, so you grant to a role and then give the role to many users. WITH GRANT OPTION lets a user pass the privilege on to others. SQLite, which is a single-file embedded database, has no user accounts and no GRANT; permissions there come from the file system.

Least privilege: Give each user or app only the rights it needs. The public result website needs SELECT on a results view, never DELETE on anything. If that website is ever hacked, the attacker inherits only those small rights. Combining views with GRANT is a standard way to show each group exactly the rows and columns it should see.

SQL inside programs: Apps do not type SQL into a console; they send it through a driver or library: JDBC in Java, ODBC in many languages, sqlite3 or psycopg in Python, and database packages in Dart and Flutter. The steps are always similar: open a connection, prepare a statement, bind values to parameters, execute, read the result rows, and close or reuse the connection.
