quiz.explain: Recovery itself might be interrupted; applying the same undo or redo twice must not change the result.

lessons.title: NoSQL and Distributed Databases: Beyond One Server
lessons.content:
Imagine a single shop in Dhaka that suddenly gets customers from every district, then from other countries. One shopkeeper, one counter and one register cannot keep up, no matter how fast they work. The solution is many branches, each with its own staff and records, that somehow stay in agreement. Big apps face the same problem with data. A relational database on one server works beautifully up to a point, but a social network with hundreds of millions of users, or a ride app tracking drivers every few seconds, needs data spread over many machines. This lesson covers how data is distributed, the trade-offs that come with it, and the NoSQL databases built for this world.

Scaling up versus scaling out: There are two ways to handle more load. Scaling up, or vertical scaling, means buying a bigger server: more CPU, memory and faster disks. It is simple, but there is a ceiling and the price rises steeply. Scaling out, or horizontal scaling, means adding more ordinary machines and splitting the work. It can grow much further and survive the loss of a machine, but it makes everything else harder: queries, transactions and consistency now involve the network.

Replication: Replication keeps copies of the same data on several machines. Benefits: if one machine dies, another has the data, giving high availability; and reads can be spread across copies, giving more read capacity. In a leader-follower setup, also called primary-replica, all writes go to the leader, which sends changes to the followers; reads can go anywhere. Synchronous replication waits for followers to confirm each write, which is safe but slower; asynchronous replication does not wait, which is fast, but a follower may briefly show old data, and recent writes can be lost if the leader dies before sending them.

Sharding: Sharding, also called horizontal partitioning, splits the rows of a table across machines, each holding a part called a shard. Students with ids 1 to 1,000,000 on server 1, 1,000,001 to 2,000,000 on server 2, and so on, is range sharding. Hashing the id to pick a server is hash sharding, which spreads load evenly but makes range queries visit every shard. Choosing the shard key is crucial: queries that include the key go to one shard and are fast; queries that do not must ask every shard. Real systems combine both ideas: each shard is replicated.

Adding machines and rebalancing: When a sharded system grows, data must move to the new machines. With naive hashing, such as id mod 4, adding a fifth server changes the target of most keys, so almost all data would move. Consistent hashing fixes this: servers and keys are placed on the same circle of hash values, and each key belongs to the next server clockwise. Adding a server takes over only the keys between it and its neighbour, a small fraction of the total. Many distributed key-value and column-family stores, including Cassandra, use this idea.

Distributed queries: A join between tables stored on different machines must ship data over the network, which is often slower than reading disks. So distributed optimizers count network transfer as a major cost. A classic trick is the semi-join: instead of sending a whole table to the other site, send only the distinct join-key values, let the other site keep only the rows that will match, and send those back. Placing tables that are often joined on the same shard key, so matching rows live on the same machine, avoids the problem altogether.

Distributed transactions and two-phase commit: If a transaction changes rows on two different servers, both must commit or both must abort. The classic protocol is two-phase commit, 2PC. A coordinator first sends 'prepare' to every participant; each one makes its changes durable in its log and votes yes, or votes no if it cannot. In phase two, if all voted yes, the coordinator sends 'commit'; if any voted no, it sends 'abort'. It is safe, but it has a famous weakness: if the coordinator crashes after participants voted yes, they are stuck, holding locks, unable to decide alone. That is why 2PC is called a blocking protocol, and why many large systems try to avoid distributed transactions.

The CAP theorem: In a distributed system, network links between machines can fail, splitting the machines into groups that cannot talk, called a network partition. The CAP theorem, proposed by Eric Brewer around 2000 and proved by Gilbert and Lynch in 2002, says that during a partition, a system must choose between consistency, meaning every read sees the latest write, and availability, meaning every request to a working machine gets a response. P, partition tolerance, is not really optional, because networks do fail. So the real choice is: during a partition, refuse some requests to stay consistent, or answer them and risk stale data.

CP and AP choices: A bank's balance system typically chooses consistency: it is better to show 'Service temporarily unavailable' than to let two branches each approve a withdrawal of the same money. A social network's like counter typically chooses availability: showing 1,203 likes instead of 1,205 for a few seconds harms nobody, while refusing to load the page annoys millions. When there is no partition, a system can offer both, but there is still a trade-off between consistency and latency, because waiting for other machines to agree takes time.

BASE and eventual consistency: In contrast to ACID, many distributed NoSQL systems describe themselves as BASE: Basically Available, Soft state, Eventually consistent. Eventual consistency means that if no new updates happen, all replicas will eventually hold the same value, but in the meantime different replicas may answer differently. Some systems let you tune this per request using quorums: with N copies, a write waits for W of them and a read asks R of them; if R + W is greater than N, every read overlaps with every write and sees the latest value.

Weaker guarantees users still expect: Even an eventually consistent system should give some common-sense promises. Read-your-writes consistency means that after you post a comment, you yourself will see it, even if friends see it a moment later; systems often achieve this by sending your reads to the leader for a short time after you write. Monotonic reads mean you never see data go back in time, for example a like count dropping from 1,205 to 1,203 on refresh. These smaller guarantees make an eventually consistent app feel normal to its users.

What NoSQL means: NoSQL is a loose name, often read as 'not only SQL', for databases that do not use the relational table model as their main structure. They grew popular in the late 2000s, when web companies needed huge scale, flexible data shapes and high availability. There are four main families: key-value, document, column-family and graph stores. Many now support some SQL-like querying and some transactions, so the line between SQL and NoSQL is blurrier than it once was.

Key-value stores: The simplest model: a giant dictionary from keys to values. You can put a value under a key, get it back, and delete it, very fast, often from memory. The database does not look inside the value. Redis is a popular example, widely used for caching, session storage, counters and leaderboards. Use it when you always look things up by a known key, such as a session id or a user's shopping cart.

Document stores: A document store keeps self-describing documents, usually JSON-like, each with its own fields and possibly nested lists. A student document might hold name, department and a list of enrollments inside it, so one read fetches everything for a profile page, with no joins. Different documents in the same collection can have different fields. MongoDB is a well-known example. Document stores suit data that is naturally read as a whole unit, like a product with variable attributes; they are weaker when data is heavily shared and related across documents.

Column-family stores: Also called wide-column stores, they organize data into rows identified by a key, with many columns grouped into families, and each row can have different columns. They are designed for huge write volumes spread across many machines. Apache Cassandra and HBase are examples, used for things like sensor readings, message histories and activity logs. Data is usually modelled around the queries you will run, often duplicating it in several tables, each shaped for one query.

Graph databases: A graph database stores nodes, such as people, places or products, and edges, such as 'friend of', 'lives in' or 'bought', with properties on both. Queries follow edges: friends of friends who like cricket, or the shortest path between two stations. In a relational database, such multi-hop queries need many self-joins; in a graph database, following edges is the basic operation. Neo4j is a well-known example, used for social networks, recommendation and fraud detection.

SQL versus NoSQL, how to choose: Choose a relational database when data is structured and related, when you need joins, constraints and strong ACID transactions, such as for banking, inventory, accounts and student records. This is the right default for most applications. Choose a NoSQL store when a specific need dominates: massive scale with simple access patterns, very flexible or nested data, extremely low latency lookups, or graph-shaped questions. Many real systems use both: a relational database as the source of truth, plus Redis for caching and a search engine for full-text search. This is sometimes called polyglot persistence.

Real-life example 1, a ride-sharing app: Driver locations change every few seconds for thousands of drivers. Storing them in a key-value or in-memory store keyed by driver id gives fast updates and lookups. Trips and payments, which involve money and must be exact, go into a relational database with full ACID transactions. The map of nearby drivers can tolerate being a second out of date; the fare charged to a rider cannot. Choosing different stores for different consistency needs is exactly the CAP trade-off in practice.

Real-life example 2, a national e-commerce site during a sale: Product catalogue pages, with many different attributes for phones, clothes and groceries, fit a document model and are cached heavily. Orders and stock levels need consistency, so they live in a relational database, sharded by order id or region, with replicas for reads. If one data centre loses its network link, the site might keep showing products from a replica, choosing availability, but refuse to confirm orders until it can be sure stock is correct, choosing consistency for the part that handles money.

Common mistakes and exam favourites: Saying NoSQL is always faster or always better at scale; it is better for specific access patterns and often gives up joins and strong consistency. Reading CAP as 'pick any two of three'; partitions are not optional, so the choice is consistency or availability during a partition. Confusing replication, which copies the same data, with sharding, which splits different data. Forgetting that 2PC can block if the coordinator fails. Typical exam questions: compare SQL and NoSQL, describe the four NoSQL families with examples, explain CAP and BASE, explain 2PC, and contrast replication with sharding.

Recap: Scaling out spreads data over many machines through replication, which copies data for availability and read capacity, and sharding, which splits data for write capacity and size. Distributed transactions use two-phase commit, which is safe but can block. The CAP theorem says that during a network partition, a system must choose consistency or availability. BASE systems accept eventual consistency, which quorums can tune. NoSQL stores come in four families: key-value, document, column-family and graph, each fitting particular access patterns, while relational databases remain the right default for structured, related data. Next lesson closes the course with security, data warehouses and a full recap.
key_points: Scaling up buys a bigger server; scaling out adds more machines and makes queries and transactions distributed.
Replication copies the same data to several machines for availability and read capacity; sharding splits different rows across machines.
Two-phase commit: prepare and vote, then commit or abort; it is blocking if the coordinator fails.
CAP: during a network partition, a system must choose consistency or availability.
BASE systems are eventually consistent; with quorums, R + W > N ensures reads see the latest write.
NoSQL families: key-value (Redis), document (MongoDB), column-family (Cassandra, HBase), graph (Neo4j).
Relational databases remain the default for structured, related data needing ACID; many systems combine several stores.
lessons.tip: For each NoSQL family, remember one example product and one typical use: Redis for caching sessions, MongoDB for product catalogues, Cassandra for sensor or message logs, Neo4j for friend recommendations. Exam answers with concrete examples score better than definitions alone.
lessons.task: Design the data storage for a food delivery app in your city. Decide which data goes into a relational database, which into a key-value store, and which could use a document store, and explain each choice. Then describe what the app should do with restaurant menus and with payments if one data centre loses network contact.

quiz.q: What is the difference between replication and sharding?
options: Replication splits data; sharding copies it
Replication copies the same data to several machines; sharding splits different data across machines
Replication is only for NoSQL; sharding is only for SQL
quiz.explain: Replicas hold the same data for availability; shards hold different parts of the data for scale.

quiz.q: According to the CAP theorem, what must a distributed system choose during a network partition?
quiz.explain: Partitions cannot be ruled out, so during one the system either refuses some requests to stay consistent or answers them and risks stale data.

quiz.q: Which is the main weakness of two-phase commit?
options: It cannot handle more than two servers
Participants can be blocked if the coordinator fails after they vote yes
quiz.explain: Prepared participants cannot decide alone, so they wait, holding locks, until the coordinator recovers.

quiz.q: Which kind of database fits 'find friends of friends who like cricket' most naturally?
quiz.explain: Graph databases store relationships as edges and make following several hops the basic operation.

quiz.q: With N = 3 replicas, which quorum setting guarantees that every read sees the latest write?
quiz.explain: R + W = 4 is greater than N = 3, so every read set overlaps every write set.

lessons.title: Security, Data Warehouses and Course Wrap-up
lessons.content:
A bank vault is not protected by one lock. There is a guard at the door who checks who you are, a list of who may open which locker, cameras recording every visit, and thick walls so that even a stolen key is not enough. Databases need the same layers, because they hold the most valuable data a company has: money, health records, exam results, national ID numbers. This final lesson covers database security, then looks at a different use of data, analysis in data warehouses, and ends with a recap of the whole course so you can see how all 25 lessons fit together.

Security goals: Database security protects three things, often called CIA. Confidentiality: only authorized people can read data, so your medical history is not visible to random staff. Integrity: only authorized people can change data, and only in allowed ways, so nobody can quietly raise their own exam marks. Availability: authorized people can use the data when they need it, so attacks or failures do not lock out a hospital at night. Each security feature serves one or more of these goals.

Authentication: Authentication answers 'who are you?' Users log in with a username and password, and increasingly with a second factor, like a code sent to a phone, or with certificates for programs. A database should never store passwords as plain text; it should store a salted hash, produced by a slow password-hashing function such as bcrypt or Argon2, so that a stolen table does not reveal the passwords. Applications should connect with their own database accounts, never with the all-powerful administrator account.

Authorization and privileges: Authorization answers 'what may you do?' SQL uses GRANT and REVOKE, as you saw in lesson 12: GRANT SELECT ON student TO advisor; GRANT SELECT, UPDATE (grade) ON enroll TO teacher; REVOKE UPDATE ON enroll FROM teacher. Privileges can be on whole tables, on specific columns, or on views, which lets you show only certain rows and columns. The principle of least privilege says each user and program should get only the privileges it truly needs, so a mistake or a stolen password causes limited damage.

Roles: Granting privileges to hundreds of people one by one is error-prone. A role is a named bundle of privileges: CREATE ROLE teacher; GRANT SELECT, UPDATE (grade) ON enroll TO teacher; then GRANT teacher TO rahim, karim. When a new teacher joins, one GRANT gives them everything; when someone leaves, one REVOKE removes it. This is role-based access control, and it is how most organizations manage database permissions. Privileges can also be passed on WITH GRANT OPTION, but that should be used carefully, because revoking later can cascade.

SQL injection: The most famous database attack. Suppose a login page builds a query by gluing user input into a string: 'SELECT * FROM student WHERE name = '' + input + '''. If the user types ' OR '1'='1, the query becomes WHERE name = '' OR '1'='1', which is true for every row. In our test database, this glued-together query returned all 5 students instead of none. Worse inputs can drop tables or read password columns. Injection has caused many real data breaches, and it still appears regularly in security reports.

Preventing injection: The fix is prepared statements, also called parameterized queries: SELECT * FROM student WHERE name = ? with the input passed separately as a parameter. The database treats the parameter purely as a value, never as SQL code, so ' OR '1'='1 is just a strange name that matches nobody. In our test, the parameterized version returned 0 rows for the same input. Extra layers help too: validate input, use least-privilege accounts so even a successful injection cannot drop tables, and never show raw database error messages to users.

Encryption: Encryption protects data if someone gets the bytes without permission. Encryption in transit, with TLS, protects data travelling between the application and the database, so nobody on the network can read it. Encryption at rest protects data files and backups on disk, so a stolen disk or backup tape is useless without the key. Very sensitive columns, such as national ID numbers, can be encrypted individually. The keys must be stored separately from the data, or the protection is meaningless.

Auditing and other protections: Auditing records who did what and when: logins, failed logins, changes to grades or balances. Triggers from lesson 12 can write simple audit logs, and most database systems have built-in audit features. Logs help discover attacks and settle disputes. Backups, from lesson 23, protect availability against ransomware that encrypts data and demands payment. Statistical databases that publish only totals must also be careful, because combining many aggregate queries can sometimes reveal an individual's data.

Views as a security tool: Views from lesson 11 are one of the simplest security tools. Instead of giving an advisor access to the whole student table, you can create a view that shows only the name, department and CGPA of students in the advisor's department, and grant SELECT on that view only. The advisor never sees phone numbers or addresses, and never sees students from other departments. Some systems go further with row-level security, where the database itself automatically adds a filter to every query based on who is logged in.

OLTP versus OLAP: So far, most of this course has been about online transaction processing, OLTP: many small, fast transactions that read and write a few rows, like transfers, enrollments and orders. Online analytical processing, OLAP, is different: few but huge queries that read millions of rows to answer questions like 'total sales by district per month for the last three years'. Running such queries on the busy OLTP database would slow down customers. So organizations copy data into a separate system built for analysis.

Data warehouses: A data warehouse is a large database that collects historical data from many operational systems, cleaned and organized for analysis. It is subject-oriented, organized around topics like sales or students; integrated, combining data from different sources into one consistent format; time-variant, keeping history for years; and non-volatile, mostly loaded and read, rarely updated. Decision makers use it to see trends and plan.

ETL: Data reaches the warehouse through ETL: Extract, Transform, Load. Extract pulls data from sources, such as the sales database, the HR system and spreadsheets. Transform cleans and reshapes it: fixing spellings like 'Chittagong' versus 'Chattogram', converting currencies and dates, removing duplicates, and computing summary values. Load writes it into the warehouse, usually in scheduled batches, such as every night. Data cleaning in the transform step often takes most of the effort in a warehouse project.

Star schema: Warehouses usually use a star schema. In the centre is a fact table holding measurements of events, such as each sale: quantity, amount, plus foreign keys. Around it are dimension tables that describe the context: product, store, customer and date, with attributes such as category, district and month. Queries join the fact table with a few dimensions and group by dimension attributes. A snowflake schema normalizes the dimensions further, splitting district into a separate region table, for example; it saves space but needs more joins. Warehouses deliberately accept some redundancy in dimensions for simpler, faster queries, unlike the normalization rules of lessons 14 and 15.

OLAP operations: Analysts think of warehouse data as a cube with dimensions like product, place and time. Roll-up summarizes to a coarser level, from daily to monthly sales. Drill-down goes to finer detail, from district totals to individual stores. Slice fixes one dimension, such as only the year 2025; dice picks a sub-cube with several conditions. Pivot rotates the view, swapping rows and columns. SQL supports this with GROUP BY plus extensions like ROLLUP and CUBE in many systems, and warehouses use column storage and bitmap indexes, from lesson 17, to make it fast. Data mining then searches warehouse data for patterns, such as products often bought together.

Real-life example 1, a university portal: Students log in with authentication; advisors have a role that can read their advisees' records through a view; teachers can update only the grade column of enroll, for their own courses. All queries use parameters, so a student typing a quote into the search box cannot inject SQL. Grade changes are audited by a trigger, so if a grade changes after publication, the log shows who did it and when. Each of these is a small step, and together they make the system trustworthy.

Real-life example 2, a retail chain's warehouse: Every night, ETL extracts the day's sales from hundreds of outlet systems, cleans product names and district spellings, and loads them into a star schema with sales facts and product, outlet and date dimensions. The next morning, managers roll up sales by division, drill down into the outlets with falling sales, and slice by the Eid season to plan stock for next year. Meanwhile, the stores' OLTP systems keep processing customers at full speed, untouched by these heavy queries.

The whole course in one map: Lessons 1 and 2 explained why DBMSs exist and how they are built in layers. Lessons 3 to 6 covered modelling: ER diagrams, mapping to tables, the relational model and relational algebra. Lessons 7 to 12 taught SQL, from creating tables to joins, subqueries, views, triggers, privileges and programs. Lessons 13 to 15 covered design theory: functional dependencies and normal forms up to BCNF and 4NF. Lessons 16 to 19 opened the engine: storage, indexes, query processing and optimization. Lessons 20 to 23 covered transactions, serializability, concurrency control and recovery. Lesson 24 went beyond one server, and this lesson added security and analytics.

How it fits together: When you click 'Pay' in an app, every part of this course works at once. Authentication and privileges check who you are and what you may do. A prepared SQL statement, written against a well-normalized schema designed from an ER model, is parsed, optimized using statistics and run with indexes over pages in the buffer pool. It runs inside a transaction protected by locks or versions, logged ahead so a crash cannot lose it, perhaps replicated to another city. That night, ETL copies it into a warehouse where managers analyse it. Seeing this full chain is the real goal of a DBMS course.

Common mistakes and exam favourites: Building SQL by string concatenation with user input. Giving applications the administrator account. Confusing authentication, who you are, with authorization, what you may do. Running heavy analytics on the live OLTP database. Assuming warehouses must be fully normalized like OLTP schemas. Typical exam questions: explain SQL injection with an example and its prevention; write GRANT, REVOKE and role statements; compare OLTP and OLAP; draw a star schema for a given business; explain ETL; and define roll-up, drill-down, slice and dice.

Recap: Database security protects confidentiality, integrity and availability through authentication, authorization with GRANT, REVOKE and roles, least privilege, prepared statements against SQL injection, encryption in transit and at rest, auditing and backups. Analysis runs separately in data warehouses, fed by ETL and organized as star or snowflake schemas, with OLAP operations like roll-up and drill-down. With this, you have seen a database from its design and SQL down to pages, indexes, plans, transactions, logs and distributed copies. Build a small project that uses them together, and the whole course will come to life.
key_points: Security goals are confidentiality, integrity and availability.
Authentication checks who you are; authorization, with GRANT, REVOKE and roles, controls what you may do; follow least privilege.
SQL injection happens when user input is glued into SQL text; prepared statements with parameters prevent it.
Encrypt data in transit with TLS and at rest on disks and backups; keep keys separate; audit sensitive actions.
OLTP runs many small transactions; OLAP runs few large analytical queries, usually on a separate data warehouse.
ETL extracts, transforms (cleans) and loads data into the warehouse; star schemas have a fact table surrounded by dimension tables.
OLAP operations: roll-up, drill-down, slice, dice and pivot.
lessons.tip: In every project from now on, make two habits automatic: always use parameterized queries, and always create a separate database user for your application with only the privileges it needs. These two habits alone prevent a large share of real database breaches.
lessons.task: Design a star schema for a mobile recharge business: a fact table for recharges and at least three dimension tables. Write one query that rolls up recharge amounts by division and month. Then write the GRANT statements for an analyst role that may only read the warehouse, and explain how you would keep the recharge app safe from SQL injection.

quiz.q: A login form builds SQL by joining strings, and a user types ' OR '1'='1. What is the attack, and what prevents it?
options: Denial of service; prevented by backups
SQL injection; prevented by prepared statements with parameters
Phantom read; prevented by SERIALIZABLE isolation
quiz.explain: The input changes the SQL logic; with parameters, the database treats it as a plain value.

quiz.q: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
options: Authentication checks who you are; authorization decides what you may do
Authentication encrypts data; authorization backs it up
Authorization checks passwords; authentication grants privileges
quiz.explain: Logging in proves identity; GRANT and roles then control the allowed actions.

quiz.q: What does a role provide in SQL security?
options: A named bundle of privileges that can be granted to many users at once
quiz.explain: Roles make managing permissions for many users simple and consistent.

quiz.q: Which statement best describes OLAP compared with OLTP?
options: Few large queries reading many rows for analysis
quiz.explain: OLAP queries scan and summarize large amounts of historical data, unlike short OLTP transactions.

quiz.q: In a star schema, what is in the central table?
options: Facts, such as sale amounts, with foreign keys to dimension tables
Only descriptive attributes like product names
quiz.explain: The fact table holds measurements of events and links to dimensions like product, store and date.
